articles.title: Why the internet loves football star Erling Haaland | CNN
articles.summary: Norwegian striker Erling Haaland is winning fans far beyond the pitch this World Cup season, thanks to his surprisingly relatable, unfiltered online persona.
articles.body:
Norwegian striker Erling Haaland is winning fans far beyond the pitch this World Cup season, thanks to his surprisingly relatable, unfiltered online persona.

Videos showing a person dressed up as Cat in the Hat roaming streets after dark have spread across social media, even prompting responses from police in Ireland and the UK. But it remains unclear which, if any, of the sightings are real or if they are AI-generated.

Kirk Heilbrun, a psychologist called by the prosecution , testified that he concluded Lindsay Clancy was not psychotic when she killed her three children and understood her actions were wrong. Helibrun told the court his "clinical opinion is that she was criminally responsible on January 24th." Defense attorneys for Clancy, who is charged with murder, argue she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and extreme mental illness and should not be held criminally responsible for the killings.

Justin Lester, a pastor in Vallejo, California created an "AI twin" so his constituents could have access to him 24/7. CNN's Nick Watt speaks to him about how it works.

Target is facing backlash for selling a children’s Halloween costume depicting a circus clown that critics said evoked blackface and minstrel shows. The company announced it pulled the item and acknowledged the issue in an apology.

Natalie Harp’s now-inactive Twitter feed shows a non-stop thread of posts showing devotion to President Donald Trump. These posts were on her account years before she became a White House aide to the president, posting more than 150 tweets on January 6, 2021, alone, in support of the president. CNN's Isabelle Chapman reports.

Capybaras, penguins and even giant snails were weighed and measured as London Zoo carried out its annual health checks. The data helps keep track of the animals’ health and contributes to a global conservation database.

Divine, a new app inspired by six-second video platform Vine, launched last week and already has about 100,000 users, according to its founder. CNN’s Matias Grez looks at what you can do on the app and how it stands apart from other mainstream social media platforms. Divine is not formally affiliated with Vine.

articles.title: Germany were once World Cup kings. Now they're simply not that good
articles.summary: Germany were knocked out of the World Cup by Paraguay on penalties; Kai Havertz cancelled out Julio Enciso's early opener but missed his spot-kick in the shoot-out; Nick Woltemade and Jonathan Tah also missed penalties, after the latter had a late goal disallowed by VAR
articles.body:
Sure, big teams have been upset by smaller teams before - the World Cup would not be the most watched sporting drama on the planet if everyone knows the ending - and star players have missed penalties in shoot-outs before.

No, they were exempt from such jeopardy and public humblings. They were for everyone else - English teams and players, for example.

If you are under the age of, let's say 20, though, you might be shaking your head at this point, thinking, "Come off it, Slater, you are pulling my leg - Germany ain't all that".

And you would be right. Something changed.

When Germany beat Argentina in 2014 to claim their fourth World Cup title in 17 attempts, it capped a four-tournament run since 2002 that had seen them finish second, third, third and then first. It also came five days after they beat the hosts Brazil in arguably the World Cup's most shocking final score: 7-1.

At that point, only the most shameless Brazilian would have argued with the idea that Germany were the World Cup's top nation. OK, Brazil had one more star on their jersey than Germany but Germany had also been runner-up four times and had won four third-fourth play-off matches.

Add all that up and Germany have finished on FIFA's podium 12 times - three more than any other nation. So, their highs were higher than almost every other nation's and their lows were higher than everyone's.

Since then? Welcome to everyone else's world, Die Mannschaft, where disappointment is on tap.

They failed to get out of the group at the 2018 World Cup in Russia, losing against Mexico and South Korea either side of a scratchy win over Sweden. In Qatar, four years later, they lost their opener to Japan, drew with Spain and beat Costa Rica, but by then their fate was out of their hands as they failed to reach the knockout rounds.

At least they managed that here, I suppose, but that is where the consolations must finish. Losing against Paraguay, who were ripped apart by the United States two weeks ago and are currently ranked 34th in the world, is a disaster for Deutschland.

"This is the third elimination in a row and that means we are not part of the first-class teams anymore," said Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann afterwards, not knowing whether to sound defiant or downtrodden - these humiliations are all so new, you see.

"When you exit the World Cup against Paraguay, it's very bitter. If you don't score enough goals, some teams can hurt you."

Neither team looked capable of hurting anyone for the first 42 minutes of this one but Paraguay took the lead with the first decent move of the game. Germany cleared a corner but Miguel Almiron picked up the loose ball, shaped to cross but found the overlapping Matias Galarza (his Atlanta United team-mate last season) with a lovely reverse pass. His first-time cross found Strasbourg forward Julio Enciso's forehead and Paraguay were 1-0 up.

Nagelsmann sent his team out a few minutes early and that appeared to poke them from their slumber. Their equaliser came nine minutes into the second half when Arsenal's Kai Havertz flicked on a fine, early cross from Liverpool's Florian Wirtz.

I mention their club sides on purpose. Paraguay's squad is comprised of guys who are no longer considered good enough to play for one of Europe's top teams or never got the chance in the first place. They play in Argentina, Brazil, and the U.S.. Germany's squad, on the other hand, comes from the top sides in the Bundesliga and Premier League.

With the scores level, most experienced World Cup-watchers relaxed a little. There would be no history made here today, I thought to myself, and started to think about which restaurant I might make for dinner.

However, the second goal never came. OK, it probably did come, but the video assistant referee from Nicaragua did not like the way Waldemar Anton looked at Paraguay goalkeeper Orlando Gill, so she told referee Jalal Jayed to see for himself. Whatever it was, he saw it, too, and Jonathan Tah's back-post header was chalked off.

What we did get, though, was some very stout Paraguayan defending, particularly from centre-backs Jose Canale and Gustavo Gomez, who headed away almost everything Germany threw at them, despite being half a foot shorter than the giants Nagelsmann was sending on.

"The opponent was a bit shaky after the equaliser but we didn't do enough when we went to two strikers; not enough crosses," said Nagelsmann.

Erm, there were plenty of crosses, Julian. The other team just headed them away.

"It has to be said, Paraguay defended very well," he later admitted.

But then we got to Monday's main turn-up-for-the-books: German inefficiency from 12 yards.

Havertz stepped up to take the first penalty. Jayed made him wait for longer than seemed necessary and Gill did the rest, saving to his left. It was the first German miss in a penalty shoot-out since 1982. They had scored 15 in a row.

The new streak was two when Gill saved Nick Woltemade's fourth penalty. That gave Paraguay two attempts to win it - attempts they squandered, which suggests even they were confused by what was going on.

However, Tah then put his sudden-death penalty into orbit, giving Canale the chance to give everyone in Paraguay a day off and send Germany home.

"Everybody is very sad but I don't put the blame on any of the players who missed the penalties," said Nagelsmann. "It happens to big players all the time and it happened to big players today."

Havertz, so often the man for the grand occasion in club football, was crestfallen.

"I want to apologise because this is my second World Cup and we have failed twice," the Arsenal star said. "We are all very disappointed because we had many plans for this World Cup and it is not a good feeling to go out so early. We tried to hurt them out wide but it didn't really work out and I don't think we deserved to win.

"We played good football but something was always missing throughout the tournament, and it was the same today. As players, we need to look at ourselves and see what we can do better."

Mainz midfielder Nadiem Amiri was an extra-time substitute and he did what he was brought on to do: score his penalty. Maybe that is why he was a little more positive than Havertz and Nagelsmann, although this a very relative statement.

"We have a lot of young players with a lot of quality," said Amiri. "But at the moment, to think about the future is the wrong decision. I feel for everybody. It was very sad, a shocking end to the game, and it's very difficult to find the right words."

That job is probably the German FA's, the DFB.

"I won't step down," said Nagelsmann. "If the DFB want me to continue, I'll continue, but I know how the industry works. I know a lot of people will want me to leave now but I'll continue if the DFB wants me to stay.

"If we were to do a survey in Germany today, the German people won't speak very positively about me. We haven't done much in this tournament for people to celebrate. I know that not everyone in Germany will agree with me staying on."

When asked for his take on what went wrong, the former RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich boss said he had some ideas but was not going to go into them now. He did, however, suggest that Germany did not have any left-backs once Nico Schlotterbeck got injured.

Not enough fit full-backs you say? Sounds familiar.

But a shortage at one particular position does not sound like a reasonable explanation for 12 years of relative failure. Germany had won 75 per cent of all the games they had ever played at the World Cup when they came off the field in Rio de Janeiro in 2014. They have won only 40 per cent of them since, and their record at the Euros has been very similar.

This is why they have not been higher than ninth in FIFA's world rankings since 2018 and will be plummeting into the teens now. Germany are simply not that good anymore.

The last time something like this happened, when they went out of the 1998 World Cup and 2000 Euros early, the DFB embarked on a radical overhaul of the German youth development system, revamped the team's tactics, trained a new generation of coaches, and immediately started winning again. Former The Athletic writer Raphael Honigstein wrote a very good book about it, Das Reboot .

Raphael, it is time for a reboot of the reboot. There could be a sequel in it.

articles.title: World Cup 2026: Is the penalty stutter at risk after Mbappe, Brazil, Germany and Netherlands setbacks?
articles.summary: Stuttered penalty run-ups have given players a boost of up to 10 per cent in the Premier League - but the technique has converted at only 53 per cent during the 2026 World Cup
articles.body:
That question gained fresh weight on Thursday night, when Bono saved Kylian Mbappe's stuttered penalty in France's 2-0 win over Morocco .

Stuttering during a penalty run-up can give takers a boost of as much as 10 per cent compared to traditional methods, according to analysis of five years' worth of Premier League penalties undertaken by leading football psychology professor Geir Jordet.

The advantage of the technique has been deemed so excessive that the laws of the game were amended in 2016 to prevent players from making goalkeepers dive early by feinting with their final touch - though that did little to curtail its success.

The stutter has felt the ire of fans' frustrations for much of that time. It is difficult to fully define why, beyond a perceived level of unnecessary added theatrics. And when things go wrong, an acrobatic run-up presents an easy target. Just ask Eberechi Eze after the Champions League final.

And following high-profile shoot-out exits for Germany and Netherlands at this World Cup, both including stutters from the losing side, that exasperation has reached what may be a peak. But there are signs of a growing justification behind those grievances.

Of the 19 stuttered penalty run-ups at this World Cup, nine have resulted in missed spot-kicks. The conversion rate has edged above 50 per cent, but only just - and remains well below the 71 per cent success rate for non-stuttered penalties.

Why? Goalkeepers have begun to fight back. And not before time.

"The majority of the top, top penalty takers in the world use the stutter," Jordet, whose book Pressure explains the psychology behind penalties, tells Sky Sports . "And until quite recently, goalkeepers have struggled against this.

"It seems crazy to say it, but they haven't had effective counter-measures. I've seen professional analysts for big clubs and national teams getting their analysis completely wrong by just reducing a penalty taker to direction.

"But with and without a stutter technique is a completely different technique, even with the same placement."

Netherlands' shoot-out loss presents a perfect case study because of the role of Morocco goalkeeper Bono, long admired for his hoodoo over penalties with eight of the previous 12 he had faced being missed.

He has refused to be coaxed into moving early, instead turning the uncertainty back onto the penalty taker by feinting to go one way in response to a stutter but diving the other - or in some cases, feinting twice. Arguably, he has deployed the goalkeeping equivalent of the same technique he has to face.

"He has this ability to get into penalty takers' minds, and sow some doubt about themselves and their technique. That's quite a feat as a goalkeeper," says Jordet.

Bono's bluffing planted enough doubt into Justin Kluivert's mind for the Netherlands winger to miss the goal entirely after a stuttered spot-kick.

His high jinks during Crysencio Summerville's penalty put the West Ham winger off too. But this is just the latest step on a wider goalkeeping redemption arc he has been leading for some time.

And he did it again against France. Mbappe's stuttered attempt was saved by Bono, even if Morocco could not turn that moment into another knockout escape.

"I first noticed Bono when he faced a penalty from my countryman Erling Haaland in 2021," adds Jordet. "Bono faked twice which way he was going to go up against Haaland's stutter, and he saved the penalty.

"He had been just off his line and Haaland retook it, but he still almost saved that one too. After that, Haaland changed his approach completely."

Bono has other impressive scalps. Ivan Toney, England's penalty specialist at this World Cup, has been labelled the best spot-kick taker on the planet and prides himself on waiting for a goalkeeper to blink first before picking his spot.

But the Moroccan's technique thwarted him when the two faced each other in a penalty shoot-out in the Saudi King's Cup earlier this year, with Toney's missed kick decisive in his side's defeat.

The forward was so rattled by Bono's technique that he, too, altered his style in response - and missed another in his next game.

"This is an arms race," says Jordet. "It's about staying ahead. We need a bigger sample size but from the start of this World Cup, the goalkeepers are winning.

"If you think what brought you success six months or a year ago is going to be enough today, you're probably going to lose this race.

"I spoke to Robert Lewandowski a few years ago, who traditionally has been a huge spokesperson for the stuttered approach - and he had a good run of about 10 years in the Bundesliga where goalkeepers would just go down for him.

"But even when I spoke to him, he had a realisation he needed to adapt. He knew goalkeepers were about to catch up with him."

So what more can penalty takers do? Sadly for critics of the stutter, it probably still has a future. Even the success rate of a good old-fashioned penalty into the corner drops to about 55 per cent if a goalkeeper guesses the right way. Little better than the flip of a coin.

Theoretically, there is always room for a whole new technique - the next Panenka, or an alternative to the stutter. But the laws of the game are so prescriptive that the prospect of creating something completely different is severely limited.

Realistically, the revolution comes back to what made the stutter so successful in the first place. Keeping goalkeepers guessing.

"It's about being unpredictable, being difficult to read - so the goalkeepers don't know what's coming," says Jordet.

"Mikel Oyarzabal is excellent at this. He has mastered finding the corner, he's mastered the stuttered run-up, sometimes he just hits it high - sometimes he does a Panenka.

"It's impossible to know what's coming, he doesn't give away any clues until he does his run-up."

Mbappe had been another player bucking trends - until Bono added him to the list of stuttered run-ups stopped at this World Cup.

The Frenchman has flown in the face of advice to avoid beginning his run-up too quickly after the referee's whistle - generally associated with hurried penalties from nervous takers.

"He has a technique somewhere in between depending on the goalkeeper and not, as well," adds Jordet. "His gaze is locked onto the goalkeeper as he runs up to say to him, I think, that he sees him and wants to keep him still as long as possible.

"When he gets to the ball, he's decided where to shoot it. And he doesn't make that decision based on anything the goalkeeper might do in the build-up."

Whatever happens, this World Cup has likely not heard the end of the penalty stutter.

Not just because of its continued derision from the stands, but because of the role it will still play as penalty styles evolve - potentially, even as this tournament progresses.

"Information is travelling so fast now, there's a velocity of adoption of it that we've never seen before in the world," Jordet says.

"So we're probably going to see a development within this World Cup, I expect. After all, that is what World Cups are for, right?"

articles.title: La UEFA no continuará con la 'Ley Vinicius'
articles.standfirst: El organismo europeo defiende que dicha medida limita la libertad de expresión de los jugadores
articles.summary: El organismo europeo defiende que dicha medida limita la libertad de expresión de los jugadores
articles.body: La llamada 'Ley Vinicius' ha dado mucho de qué hablar en esta edición del Mundial. Ya son dos los jugadores que han sido expulsados por esta medida: Miguel Almirón fue la primera víctima e Hincapié la más reciente, tras una discusión con el mexicano Santi Giménez. Cada vez que suceden estos episodios, la polémica se convierte en el centro de atención. Sin embargo, la UEFA ha confirmado que no aplicará dicha norma en sus competiciones, rechazando así la medida de la FIFA para la cita mundialista. El 'caso Vinicius-Prestianni' ha marcado un antes y un después en el reglamento del fútbol mundial. Es por ello que la FIFA ha querido adoptar esta norma, entre otras medidas innovadoras que buscan reducir la pérdida de tiempo, para que no se repitan episodios como el ocurrido en la Champions League durante el partido entre el Real Madrid y el Oporto. No obstante, los jugadores que decidan taparse la boca en la Champions y en las diferentes competiciones de la UEFA no serán expulsados. El organismo europeo ha optado por desmarcarse de la regla porque defiende que limita la libertad de expresión de los futbolistas. Esto revela un capítulo más del pulso entre el organismo de Gianni Infantino y el de Aleksander Ceferin, quienes toman caminos diferentes en varios aspectos, sobre todo en los relacionados con la materia arbitral.

articles.title: World Cup 2026: How Michael Olise has become a star that shuns limelight
articles.summary: A footballer who dislikes too much media attention, but Michael Olise might not have much choice if he carries on his World Cup heroics.
articles.body:
Michael Olise is not your typical footballer.

Born and raised in England, he is setting this World Cup alight with France.

The Bayern Munich forward, via Reading and Crystal Palace, usually shuns the spotlight, loves chess, barely celebrates goals and avoids interviews - and does not have a deal with any sportswear or boot companies.

After a season with 25 goals and 28 assists for the Bundesliga champions, the 24-year-old is now seen as one of the world's best players.

Going into Saturday's last-16 tie with Paraguay, Olise has become the first player to assist five goals at one World Cup since Germany's Thomas Hassler in 1994.

Those who have known him since childhood say his reserved nature should not be seen as arrogance - it's just "Michael being Michael".

BBC offers 'Stay Up or Catch Up' for England v Mexico Published 5 July

BBC offers 'Stay Up or Catch Up' for England v Mexico

Why France's Olise is moving into Ballon d'Or picture Published 9 June

Why France's Olise is moving into Ballon d'Or picture

United, free and brilliant - can anyone stop France masterclass? Published 1 July

United, free and brilliant - can anyone stop France masterclass?

Born in London to a French-Algerian mother, Mina, and a Nigerian father, Vincent, Olise stood out from a young age.

"The sports coaches came to me one day and said have you seen this boy... in year two?" Daniel Coker, Olise's sports teacher at Dr Triplett's CE Primary School in Hayes, London, told BBC Sport.

"When I saw him play...I knew that he was going to be something special."

Coker recalled how Olise - already on Chelsea's books at the time - excelled in every sport he tried.

"At age 10 and 11 that's when I'd get him in everything I could," he added. "He'd come and have a go and just blow us out the water with how good he was."

And already the young Olise did not like any fuss.

"Michael was a quiet and shy boy. He gave so many assists to our team, he'd score loads of goals, but he didn't used to celebrate, he just used to get back straight in and want to go again," said Coker.

"He's not one of those ones to dwell on it and take that moment in. He didn't like the limelight. So when I see that on camera now, when he doesn't celebrate or he runs back, it's just what he's always done."

Headteacher Rachel Anderson remembers it being hard to get Olise back into class after football, particularly if his team hadn't won.

"He would be still kicking the ball around the classroom and it would be like, 'Come on Michael, it's enough now'," she said.

"I think other schools used to sigh and look quite depressed when we turned up with Michael on our team for so many things [different sports] because they knew they didn't stand much of a chance.

"He was a perfectionist and over-analysed everything. He was a bright boy so he did well academically."

It was also at this early age that Olise, who could also have played for England, Nigeria or Algeria, showed signs he would be picking France.

"Rachel said, 'Do you reckon he'll play for England?' I said, I don't know if we'll be lucky enough to have him play for England," Coker added.

"I think Michael really enjoyed that French culture, he went there to visit, he liked learning the language."

But it was not a straightforward path to get there.

Olise's younger brother Richard, 21, is also a professional footballer, although released this summer by Chelsea - just like Michael a decade ago.

Having briefly been at Arsenal, Olise spent seven years with Chelsea's academy before being released aged 14. He then had a short spell at Manchester City, but they too let him go.

Enter Reading, then in the Championship.

However, Brendan Flanagan, the club's head of recruitment, said he had to persuade bosses to recruit the 16-year-old in the summer of 2018.

"Because of the biases that go on in football, it took me a little bit longer to convince people in the building to bring him in because [he was] released from Chelsea, released from Man City - some people would see that as this is going to be a big problem," he told the BBC.

"What might have been deemed as Michael being problematic at other clubs, because he's quiet, he's shy, he's reserved, but we can work with those kids because that doesn't make them a bad kid, it just makes them a little bit different."

But Flanagan was afraid the Royals were going to miss out when Olise's mother said they needed some time to rebuild his confidence after the setbacks.

"She said we're going to do some work with a mentor because he's obviously low in confidence - he's been released from Chelsea, released from Man City - and we just want to make sure that when he comes in to you he's ready for you," added Flanagan.

"I thought to myself, 'That's it, end of - next time I see him he'll be playing against us somewhere'.

"Four weeks later Mina rang me to say right we're ready to go. She was true to her word - that's the kind of people they are, honest genuine people.

"He came in and we never had a single problem with him. He was without a shadow of a doubt the best player that I've ever bought into this building."

Olise was so keen to be on time for training that he would sometimes miss the start of it.

"He would come in at 7 o'clock in the morning for training, that starts at 9, and be asleep in his car when training started," Flanagan said.

Olise made his Reading debut in March, 2019, against Leeds at the age of 17 - days after joining first-team training - and went on to make 73 appearances, scoring seven goals, over three seasons.

It was also there that he got called into the French youth-team set-up.

"It wasn't a surprise that he chose France for me because they were the ones that were first in contact with him," added Flanagan.

"In that 2001 England year group, they generally tended to come from Manchester City, Chelsea, Man Utd, Arsenal, Spurs - not so many from the likes of Reading.

"Michael would be one of those that say, 'Well they chose me first, you didn't want me when I was younger, so that's where I'm going to go'."

At Reading, Olise had a release clause of Â£8m which Crystal Palace - managed then by France legend Patrick Vieira - activated in July 2021.

His Premier League quality with the Eagles was evident but initially he was much more of a provider - with 19 assists and six goals in his first two seasons.

In the summer of 2023 Chelsea activated a Â£35m release clause to re-sign the player they released as a kid.

But to the surprise of nearly everyone, Palace announced Olise had signed a new deal with them instead.

His final season at Selhurst Park was where he really found his shooting boots - netting 10 times, plus six assists, in only 19 games - and 14 starts - in a season disrupted by two different injury spells.

At the end of the 2023-24 campaign, he played for France at the Paris Olympics - under boss Thierry Henry and assistant Gael Clichy.

Former France, Arsenal and Manchester City full-back Clichy told the BBC: "I was really hoping City could actually bring him back, because he was part of the club.

"This is where I actually started to hear about him [at City]. And when he was injury-free at Palace, I started to realise who he was, what kind of player he was.

"I finally met him just before the Olympics and now the world is discovering a player that was always there, but had his own route to get there."

Before the Olympics began, Bayern announced the signing of Olise for about Â£50m.

Clubs can refuse to let players feature in the Olympics and the German side had done so with his France team-mate Mathys Tel.

But Clichy said Olise told Bayern "he had one wish - to finish the adventure of the Olympics".

"This is really the moment that stood out for us," added Clichy.

"Of course many other moments on the pitch did, but outside of the field a young player who is getting his first big move asking for that was something you don't really see.

"This is the moment we realised that he was a great player, but even more important he was a top man."

Olise helped France reach the Olympic final, where they lost to Spain in extra time.

Olise has kicked on to another level since joining Vincent Kompany's Bayern - and broke into the senior French team almost immediately.

Playing on the right wing, he followed up a campaign with 17 goals and 18 assists with one that saw 25 goals and 28 assists - a total of 88 goal involvements in two seasons.

Former France striker and BBC World Cup pundit Olivier Giroud said: "He's working hard for the team on the pitch, he's got talent but he's a team player.

"He's so relaxed when he's coming inside on his left foot, you know what he's going to do, basically like Arjen Robben back in the day."

Plenty of Olise's viral moments at Bayern include things like trying to stay out of celebrations, avoiding a TV interview and a half-hearted Bundesliga trophy lift.

He likes to walk on to the pitch with sandals before a game to check the surface.

"It's funny to see him walk with the flip-flops on the pitch casually, but this is who he is," said Clichy.

"He's very much a casual guy who has magic in his feet and knows how to express his magic."

Olise's success means he cannot avoid the limelight - and prompted talk of being a potential Ballon d'Or winner.

His chances will improve further if he can help France to glory this summer - he is only one goal off equalling Pele's record of six assists in a World Cup.

"One day Michael could be a contender for the Ballon d'Or," Giroud said.

"If you win trophies, a Ballon d'Or will come, but I think he thinks more collectively than a selfish player, and it's his personality.

"You can see on the pitch, if he can assist, he will assist, even if he could have shot to the goal. So that's what I like. He's a playmaker, but a team player, so it makes him different, special, and he can reach the top of the top."

articles.title: Julian Nagelsmann resigns as Germany head coach after shock World Cup exit with Jurgen Klopp 'ready' to take over
articles.summary: Julian Nagelsmann leaves head coach role after Germany's World Cup exit; Nagelsmann had been in charge of Germany since September 2023; German FA confirms intention to now seek talks with former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp who has confirmed his interest in replacing Nagelsmann
articles.body:
The former Liverpool boss confirmed his interest in succeeding Julian Nagelsmann and that he had been approached about the role in an interview with Magenta TV on Friday.

"Yes, I can confirm the talks," he said. "Things moved along quite quickly. Julian has resigned and the DFB is working on a successor. And in the course of these considerations, they approached me."

The German Football Association does not believe it will be an issue getting Klopp out of his current job as global head of football at Red Bull.

It would be the first time the German FA has paid a fee to appoint a coach, with Klopp having a contract with Red Bull until 2029 which includes a special exit clause for the Germany job.

Klopp said: "I have an existing contract with Red Bull. I've said many times how much I enjoy this job. As a person, I usually honour contracts. But I've also made it clear that I'm interested in talks with the DFB.

Klopp said he does not expect his current employers to stand in his way - and is ready to return to management in the capacity as a national team boss two years after his Liverpool exit.

"Now isn't the perfect timing. But it's better than it's ever been. I'm more than refuelled now, I'm ready," Klopp said.

Klopp eyeing up first managerial job in two years

Nagelsmann stepped down from the role after Germany's shock World Cup last-32 exit against Paraguay.

DFB president Bernd Neuendorf said ⁠in a statement on Friday: "The ⁠German Football Association expressly thanks Julian ‌Nagelsmann for his work since September 2023. ‌He is characterised by a high level of commitment and extraordinary ambition. ⁠Julian Nagelsmann is ​also an extremely ​responsible and sincere ​person whom we all ⁠value."

The statement added: "Regarding the appointment of a new coach, the DFB leadership will now seek talks with Jurgen Klopp. He has already signalled his general willingness to take on the position."

If Klopp makes the move it would be his first coaching job since leaving Liverpool in 2024.

Nagelsmann, 38, took charge of Germany in September 2023 and guided the nation to the Euro 2024 quarter-finals, where they were beaten by eventual winners Spain.

Germany were knocked out of the 2026 World Cup by Paraguay on penalties , following a 1-1 draw after extra-time in Boston. They had topped Group E on goal difference after thrashing newcomers Curacao 7-1 in their opening game and beating Ivory Coast 2-1, before a 2-1 defeat to Ecuador.

"I am not someone who runs away," Nagelsmann had said after the 2014 winners were dumped out.

"This is not the first time this has happened, and there are some things about today that need to be changed.

"But if the DFB wants me to continue I am going to continue. I know the mechanics of football, I know how the industry works.

"I know a lot of people will want me to leave but I would love to continue if the football association wants me to."

Klopp coaching Germany 'would be dream come true'

"It would be a dream come true that many Germans had for a lot of years.

"For more-or-less a decade, people in Germany have been talking about how good it would be if Jurgen Klopp would become the national coach and now it seems like it is going to happen.

"The DFB itself confirmed that it will talk with Jurgen Klopp in the next days - and he has already given his initial go [ahead] and said that he could imagine being Germany next national coach.

"He's still in a job in Leipzig as head of global soccer (for the Red Bull group) and there are talks that have to be made.

"But there is a good chance that Jurgen Klopp returns to the sidelines and becomes the new head coach of Germany. That's something that many, many, many Germans have wanted for years."

articles.title: La Champions 26-27 se pone en marcha en pleno Mundial
articles.standfirst: Los primeros 28 equipos arrancan la primera ronda de clasificación
articles.summary: Los primeros 28 equipos arrancan la primera ronda de clasificación
articles.body: El Mundial 2026 está entrando en su fase decisiva. Pero, en medio toda esta vorágine, la Champions League 26-27 se pone en marcha desde hoy mismo. Un total de 83 equipos repartidos entre 53 de las 55 federaciones miembro de la UEFA participarán en esta edición de la Liga de Campeones con el objetivo de suceder al PSG y levantar la 'Orejona' en el Metropolitano, que acogerá su segunda final, el próximo 5 de junio de 2027. Su entrada en la competición, eso sí, se realizará de forma progresiva. En esta primera fase, participarán 28 equipos. Según los criterios que establece la competición, 12 derrotados se irán a la segunda ronda de clasificación de la Conference League, mientras que el perdedor de las eliminatorias 4 (Lincoln vs Inter Club d'Escaldes) y 5 (Tre Fiori vs Larne) irán a la tercera fase por cuestiones organizativas. Ya desde esta primera ronda de la Champions vamos a tener representación española. Tras el excelente trabajo de Bezares en el Lincoln, Ahora ha sido Juanma Pavón quien ha recogido su testigo... mientras que Julio Velázquez tratará de llevar a lo más alto al Levski Sofia después de poner fin a 14 años de tiranía por parte del Ludogorets en Bulgaria. El equipo con más cartel en esta primera fase de la Champions, sin embargo, es el Kairat Almaty. Situados en la frontera con China, ya debutaron en la competición —jugaron contra el Real Madrid— en la pasada edición... aunque apenas lograron sumar un punto contra el Pafos en la tercera jornada. Podrán contar, al menos hasta el próximo mes de agosto, con el prometedor Dastan Satpaev, quien ya ha sido fichado por el Chelsea. Su principal competencia en la punta de lanza es Marc Gual, ex de Sevilla, Girona o Alcorcón que se ha incorporado al Kairat desde el Río Ave como agente libre. En cinco partidos, ya suma un gol y dos asistencias. Las eliminatorias se disputarán a ida y vuelta y los 14 clasificados avanzarán a una segunda ronda donde ya se ubican equipos de la altura de Dinamo Zagreb, Estrella Roja o Slovan Bratislava. Fenerbahçe, Górnik Zabrze, Sturm Graz y Hearts también arrancarán desde la Ruta de Liga. Aquí arranca la Champions.

articles.title: La Champions 26-27 echa a rodar... con marcado acento español
articles.standfirst: Se disputaron los 10 primeros partidos de la primera ronda previa
articles.summary: Se disputaron los 10 primeros partidos de la primera ronda previa
articles.body: Ya han finalizado los octavos de final y el Mundial 2026 entra en su fase decisiva. Pero, mientras termina de definirse, la Champions 26-27 ya se ha puesto en marcha con la disputa de los primeros partidos de la primera ronda previa. Aquí inicia el camino a la final que tendrá lugar en el Metropolitano el próximo 5 de junio. Ya desde el inicio de la competición, hubo marcado acento español. El Lincoln de Juan Manuel Pavón entró con buen pie y sacó un gran resultado en Gibraltar frente al Inter Club d'Escaldes (3-1), donde milita el hijo de Mauricio Pochettino, de cara al encuentro de vuelta que se disputará en Andorra. Julio Velázquez y su Levski Sofía, por su parte, acabaron rescatando un valioso empate contra el Borac (1-1) en tierras bosnias. Todo se puso en contra con el tanto de penalti transformado por Juricic a los nueve minutos de encuentro. Pero, nada más arrancar la segunda parte, Oko-Flex devolvió la igualdad al marcador. Fue el único empate del día junto al del Kauno Zalgiris frente al Drita. Fue, también, una primera tanda de partidos marcada por las tarjetas rojas. De hecho, hubo hasta cuatro expulsiones repartidas por las derrotas del Riga, Vardar y Shamrock Rovers. El Sabah, por su parte, sí sacó su encuentro adelante frente al The New Saints (2-0)... a pesar de disputar los últimos minutos con uno menos. La gran alegría de la tarde-noche de Champions se la llevó el Vikingur gracias a su victoria sobre la bocina frente al Gyor. Mañana, será turno para un Kairat Almaty que ya estuvo presente en la pasada edición de Champions. Reciben en casa al Sutjeska. Cierran la jornada Flora vs. Iberia; Petrocub vs. Egnatia; y Vitebsk vs. Universitatea.

articles.title: Marc Gual vuelve a ilusionar al Kairat Almaty con la Champions
articles.standfirst: El español anotó un gol en las instancias finales para darle la victoria al conjunto uzbeko en la ida de la primera fase previa del torneo
articles.summary: El atacante español anotó un gol en las instancias finales para darle la victoria al conjunto uzbeko
articles.body: El Kairat Almaty sigue soñando con la Champions League. El conjunto uzbeko, que fue una de las sorpresas de la competición europea la temporada pasada, está luchando en la fase previa para volver a meterse en la edición de esta campaña y de momento va en buen camino...gracias a un jugador español. Marc Gual anotó el gol que desequilibró el encuentro ante el Sutjeska macedonio en el encuentro de ida de la primera fase de clasificación. Tras un duelo igualado entre ambos conjuntos, un gol con el pecho de Lucas Áfrico en el minuto 76 dio la ventaja inicial al equipo uzbeko. Sin embargo, Marko Mrvaljevic igualó la contienda en el minuto 90, tras una asistencia de su centrocampista Deni Hocko. Cuando todo indicaba que el Sutjeska se marcharía con un empate de vuelta a Macedonia, allí emergió Marc Gual. El atacante español aprovechó un centro desde la banda derecha y el posterior salto de Edmilson para dejar pasar el balón para batir al guardameta macedonio. El camino para jugar la Champions es muy largo. El Kairat todavía tiene que ganar el segundo encuentro y tres rondas a ida y vuelta más para jugar la clasificación final. La temporada pasada lo consiguió, al imponerse de manera heroica a todo un histórico como el Celtic de Glasgow. A ver qué tal se le da en esta.

articles.title: British South Asians in Football Team of the Season 2025/26: Hamza Choudhury, Zidane Iqbal, Yan Dhanda, Mariam Mahmood all feature
articles.summary: Sky Sports News' Dev Trehan and Desi Ballers founder Zohaib Rashid pick the fourth annual combined XI, celebrating the on-field contribution made by British South Asians in football during the 2025/2026 season
articles.body:
Players from the community featured across the leagues in men's football and at every level of the English women's football pyramid.

Nine players retain their places from last year, but how does the overrall 2025/26 team shape up?

Jasbir Singh continued to lead from the back as Tamworth vice-captain, keeping eight clean sheets across the campaign and helping the Lambs claim a top-half finish in the 2025/26 National League.

Asmita Ale makes her fourth consecutive Team of the Season appearance after a solid individual campaign. Ale played 21 Women's Super League matches across the season for Leicester City.

Danny Batth rolled back the years to play an important role for unfancied Derby County last season as the club narrowly missed out on the play-offs on the last day of the season, finishing eighth in the Sky Bet Championship.

Kam Kandola had the most productive season of his career to date, playing 38 matches in a campaign where Kidderminster Harriers clinched promotion to the National League via the play-offs. Kandola has joined Hereford ahead of the new season.

Mal Benning regained his place in Shrewsbury Town's line-up after the mid-season appointment of Gavin Cowan. Benning went on to make his 500th professional career appearance and helped the club preserve its League Two status.

Millie Chandarana became an 'Invincible' for the second consecutive season, featuring prominently as Burnley went unbeaten in the league to land the title and earn promotion to Women's Super League 2. Chandarana has just signed a new deal.

Hamza Choudhury played 32 matches for Leicester City in a difficult league campaign for the Foxes but sparkled on the international stage, scoring on his home debut for Bangladesh and instantly becoming a national hero.

Zidane Iqbal appeared in the Dutch Eredivisie and the Europa League for FC Utrecht in a season where he scored his first international goal and became the first British South Asian ever to play at a World Cup, featuring in all three of Iraq's games over the summer.

Yan Dhanda emerged as a key player for Dundee following his loan switch from Hearts, featuring in 31 matches for the club and helping the Dee comfortably retain their place in the Scottish Premiership next season.

Mariam Mahmood had a fairytale season as she made her international debut for Pakistan ahead of clinching a move to Wrexham. The club won a historic league and cup double as Mahmood became the first Pakistani female to win a top-division European title.

Dilan Markanday landed a club end-of-season Player of the Year award after scoring eight goals and contributing six assists in a season where Chesterfield narrowly missed out on a League Two play-off spot.

articles.standfirst: El '9' español suma cuatro goles y dos asistencias en seis partidos con el Kairat
articles.summary: El '9' español suma cuatro goles y dos asistencias en seis partidos con el Kairat
articles.body: El Kairat dio la sorpresa la temporada pasada clasificándose para la Champions League por primera vez en su historia. Una misión (casi) imposible que aspira a reeditar gracias a los goles de Marc Gual (Badalona, 1996). "Venía de no jugar demasiado en el Río Ave, recibí varias ofertas y, tras hablar con varios compañeros que ya conocía, me decanté por la del Kairat. Es un club que lucha por títulos y por competir en Europa, que cuenta con muy buenas instalaciones y la propuesta económica también era buena. Todo era positivo, así que decidí probar y, por ahora, la verdad es que todo va muy bien", asegura a MARCA. Los 8.000 kilómetros que separan Almaty de España parecían la principal barrera: "El tema de la distancia era lo que más me tiraba para atrás. El viaje, con los dos perros, se nos hizo un poco largo a mí y a mi mujer, pero es lo único malo. Almaty es una ciudad muy 'top': moderna, bien comunicada... Tiene de todo y se vive muy bien. Hemos acertado".  Sin embargo, el exatacante de Espanyol 'B', Sevilla Atlético, Zaragoza, Girona, Real Madrid Castilla, Alcorcón, Dnipro-1, Jagiellonia Bialystok, Legia y Río Ave ha caído de pie en el Kairat: acumula cuatro goles y dos asistencias en seis partidos.  "Hasta el momento está yendo todo muy bien. He marcado goles, he repartido asistencias y, desde que llegué, no hemos perdido. El estilo de juego me viene bien: queremos tener el balón, atacar mucho, crear ocasiones...", subraya Marc Gual antes de ahondar en las exigencias tácticas de Rafael Urazbakhtin: "El míster me pide es que aparezca entre líneas para crear ocasiones y en zonas de finalización para rematarlas. Ése es mi fuerte y para lo que estoy aquí".  Marcó, también, en la victoria por 2-1 sobre el Sutjeska Niksic montenegrino en la primera ronda previa de la 'vieja' Copa de Europa. "Entrar en Champions está difícil. La temporada pasada lo consiguieron por primera vez en su historia, pero lo normal es no conseguirlo porque el nivel es muy alto y tenemos que pasar cuatro rondas previas".  La posibilidad de perpetrar un nuevo milagro, sin embargo, está ahí: "Lo vamos a intentar. Ojalá pasemos esta primera ronda para asegurarnos entrar en Europa, aunque no sea Champions, pero jugar, al menos, la Europa Legue o la Conference. Vamos paso a paso y ya llegará lo que tenga que llegar", confiesa Marc Gual, que ya compitió en el Viejo Continente con el Legia. Con el Legia, precisamente, batió su récord anotador: marcó 19 goles en la 2024-25. No va por mal camino... pero no quiere desviar el tiro. "Siempre uno quiere marcar goles, pero lo principal es ayudar al equipo, jugar, tener minutos... El resto, si el equipo va bien, irá viniendo. Ojalá pueda superar los 19 goles que marque con el Legia, pero prefiero ganar la Liga y jugar en Europa que superar mi propio récord".  Hoy, nuevamente, les espera el Sutjeska Niksic. "Los partidos de Europa y de la Liga son diferentes. En la Liga somos el equipo grande, dominamos el juego y creamos ocasiones. En Europa los partidos son más igualados y los rivales más fuertes. Hay equipos que te dominan, algo que en la Liga no pasa tan a menudo. Tenemos que adaptarnos. Eso es lo que hará que podamos entrar en Europa", reconoce el '9' español del Kairat. Con Marc 'Goal' será más fácil.

articles.title: Marc Gual y el Kairat quieren volver a estar en Champions
articles.standfirst: El conjunto kazajo selló el pase a la segunda ronda de clasificación contra el Sutjeska
articles.summary: El conjunto kazajo selló el pase a la segunda ronda de clasificación contra el Sutjeska
articles.body: El Kairat ya hizo historia la temporada pasada al convertirse en el segundo equipo kazajo en disputar la Champions tras el Astana en 2015. Sin embargo, no se conforman con ello y están dispuestos a pasearse de nuevo por los mejores campos del Viejo Continente. Un gol del ariete español Marc Gual en el tiempo de descuento amarró el triunfo contra Sutjeska en el partido de ida. "Entrar en Champions está difícil. La temporada pasada lo consiguieron por primera vez en su historia, pero lo normal es no conseguirlo porque el nivel es muy alto y tenemos que pasar cuatro rondas previas", repasaba en MARCA el ex de Río Ave en la previa del choque de vuelta. De nuevo, Rafael Urazbakhtin lo ubicó como principal referencia en el Kairat. Sin embargo, fue el jovencísimo Ismail Bakbolat (2008) quien anotó el 0-1 justo antes de abandonar el campo. El Sutjeska estaba contra las cuerdas... y firmó su sentencia con la expulsión de Raznatovic y posterior tanto de penalti de Jorginho terminaron de amarrar el pase. En la siguiente ronda ya espera el Omonisa Nicosia en el tortuoso camino que le restan a Marc Gual y el Kairat hasta poder plantarse en la fase liga definitiva de la Champions 26-27. También sellaron la clasificación el Universitatea Craiova Rumanía), el Klakvik (Islas Feroe) y el Egnatia (Albania).

articles.title: El delantero español que quiere volver a hacer historia en la Champions: "Aquí solo vale ganar"
articles.standfirst: Marc Gual, reciente fichaje del Kairat Almaty kazajo, habla de su nueva vida en Marcador Internacional de Radio MARCA
articles.summary: Marc Gual, reciente fichaje del Kairat Almaty kazajo, habla de su nueva vida en Marcador Internacional de Radio MARCA
articles.body: Marc Gual ha iniciado una nueva etapa lejos del fútbol español. El delantero catalán, de 30 años, ha fichado este verano por el Kairat Almaty, vigente campeón de Kazajistán y uno de los clubes habituales en las rondas previas de la Liga de Campeones. En una entrevista concedida a Radio MARCA en el programa Marcador Internacional, el atacante explicó los motivos que le llevaron a aceptar una aventura "desconocida", aunque reconoce que el crecimiento del club en Europa terminó de convencerle. "El año pasado no fue el mejor que he tenido, jugué menos de lo que deseaba y había que cambiar de aires. Salió esta oportunidad y nos cuadró todo. Es un equipo que pelea por títulos y que puede jugar competiciones europeas", explicó Gual, que la pasada temporada militó en el Rio Ave portugués. Su estreno no ha podido ser mejor. El Kairat ya ha superado la primera eliminatoria previa de la Champions tras eliminar al Sutjeska, con un gol decisivo del propio delantero español en el encuentro de ida. Ahora espera el Omonia de Nicosia, un rival de mayor entidad en el camino hacia la fase de liga. "Sabemos que repetir lo del año pasado es muy complicado, pero si vamos partido a partido siempre es posible. El Omonia será un rival difícil, aunque creo que tenemos equipo para competir e intentar volver a entrar en la Champions", señaló. El Kairat adquirió notoriedad internacional la pasada temporada al convertirse en el primer club kazajo en disputar la fase de liga de la Champions, donde incluso recibió la visita del Real Madrid. Aquella histórica participación ha cambiado la dimensión del club. "Los compañeros que estuvieron el año pasado dicen que todo ha cambiado. La gente te reconoce por la calle porque juegas en el Kairat y el club ha crecido muchísimo gracias a esa participación europea. Eso sí, la presión aquí no es como en otros países", reconoció. Porque, según explica Gual, la verdadera exigencia está en el campeonato doméstico. "El objetivo principal es ganar la Liga. El Kairat ha conquistado las dos últimas y es el club grande del país. Eso es lo que te permite volver a jugar las previas de la Champions". Más allá del fútbol, el delantero también habló de su adaptación a Kazajistán, un cambio radical tanto por la distancia como por la cultura. Se ha trasladado a Almaty junto a su mujer y sus dos perros, una decisión que no fue sencilla. "Era la principal duda que teníamos. Son ocho horas de vuelo y otro continente completamente diferente. Pero la ciudad nos ha sorprendido mucho, vivimos muy tranquilos y el club nos ayuda en todo con un traductor para los jugadores extranjeros", explicó. Eso sí, el mayor desafío llega con los desplazamientos europeos. "Para jugar fuera tenemos que viajar dos días antes. Entre las seis o siete horas de vuelo y el cambio horario necesitas tiempo para adaptarte", concluyó un Marc Gual que ya suma un gol en Champions y tres tantos en la liga kazaja en sus primeras semanas con el Kairat.

articles.title: Cesc, el trampolín del Como: "Cuando llegué nos cambiábamos en un bar y ahora jugamos la Champions"
articles.standfirst: El entrenador español prepara una revolución para competir en Europa
articles.summary: El entrenador español prepara una revolución para competir en Europa
articles.body: El Como prepara el más difícil todavía. La victoria sobre la Cremonese (1-4) certificó la clasificación de los 'lariani' para la Champions por primera vez en su historia.  "Es un logro enorme, conseguido con jugadores jóvenes. El presidente me dio las riendas y tomé muchas decisiones. Cuando llegué hace cuatro años, como jugador, no teníamos centro de entrenamiento y nos cambiábamos en un bar. Ahora, en cambio, estamos en Champions", recordaba Cesc Fábregas. Un hito para el que ya han puesto las bases. “No se podía dar por sentado que uno de los mejores entrenadores de Europa, como Cesc, decidiera quedarse con nosotros en el Como, al igual que Nico Paz, uno de los mejores talentos del contiente”, reconoce el director deportivo, Carlalberto Ludi. Jugar en Europa implica una importante reforma a todos los niveles, empezando por el estadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia. No sólo se aumentará el aforo, también se ampliará el terreno de juego dos metros de ancho. La plantilla sufrirá un importante cambio. La Champions únicamente te permite disponer de 17 fichas libres —sin importar nacionalidad— en la lista A. El resto, hasta 25, sólo se puede completar con futbolistas formados en la Federación a la que perteneces. Esto supone un problema. El Como, la temporada pasada, sólo contaba con dos italianos en nómina: Vigorito y Goldaniga. Entre los dos jugaron 14 minutos en Serie A. “Fichar jugadores en Italia es un problema debido a la rigidez de los métodos de pago”, asegura el presidente Mirwan Suwarso, que ha pagado seis kilos al Cantanzaro por Liberali. “El sector juvenil es crucial. Debemos permitir que el talento crezca con paciencia”, subraya Cesc. Se han ido 'pesos pesados' (Diego Carlos, Sergi Roberto, Alberto Moreno...) y han seguido pescando en LaLiga: Luis Milla y Andrés Cuenca. Vendrán más. “Si no estás preparado para jugar en el Bernabéu o el Allianz, te arriesgas a encajar seis goles. Me gusta entrenar a jóvenes, pero debemos traer gente con experiencia”, insiste Cesc. La Champions le espera.

articles.title: World Cup 2026: Will Nauru, a tiny Pacific island, finally take up football?
articles.summary: Nauru is the only nation to have never played an official international football match and hardly anyone there plays the game. Is that about to change?
articles.body:
Like everywhere, the world's smallest island nation has been gripped by football fever for the past six weeks. But once Spain lifted the World Cup trophy on Sunday, almost every trace of football on Nauru stopped.

Football is almost non-existent on this Pacific island. Nauru has never fielded a team in an official international match and it has just one â hard sand â pitch.

While there is interest in big Premier League matches, and children wear Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo kits, any attempts to actually play football tend to be mocked, unless it's Aussie rules.

But things may be slowly changing as a group of volunteers - led by British former academy player Charlie Pomroy - seek to introduce the game to what was once the world's richest nation per capita but is now heavily reliant on foreign aid and has one of the highest obesity rates in the world.

A social media post from the Nauru Soccer Federation congratulating the new world champions and setting out a dream that "one day we hope to be in Spain's position" may have been fanciful, but the groundwork is real in what it says is the last country not to have had a senior international side.

Laying the foundations, though, on an island where over-mining has left the landscape looking more like a moonscape, has been far from straightforward.

Nauru has tried to develop football previously, but it has never really taken off. The closest it has come to playing an international match was when representative teams faced a Solomon Islands expatriate team in 1994 and a refugee side in 2014.

Its complicated past goes some way to explaining why the world's most popular sport has struggled for participation.

Located in the Pacific Ocean 2,500 miles north east of Australia, Nauru's historical wealth was built on its vast deposits of phosphate from fossilised bird poo.

Nauru, which was a dependent territory of Australia until independence in 1968, was heavily mined in the late 20th Century. The minerals dried up, leaving the country once named Pleasant Island looking ragged, with large parts of its central areas uninhabitable and extremely challenging to farm.

This resulted in most of the 12,000-strong population clustering around the coastal edges with usable space at a premium on an island that measures only 21 square kilometres. And even that is shrinking, with climate change and rising sea levels threatening its very existence.

Its barren land has left the country importing more than 90% of its food â much of which is processed, contributing to 69% of the population being classed as obese and around 40% having type 2 diabetes.

One of its main sources of revenue now is from the Australian immigration detention centre it has housed for much of this century.

Everyday life on the island can be a struggle and sport has been a strong release for many, but the sport of choice is Aussie rules, which 30% of locals play. Also popular are athletics and weightlifting, which Nauru has competed in at the Olympics.

Nauru will host the Micronesian Games in 2028 â a multi-sport event that includes football and will showcase the island's desire to grow its international reputation through sport.

"They are trying to change the image for the better andâ¯get involved in more sport," says Pomroy, technical director for Nauru Soccer and one of eight volunteers aiming to develop football on the island.

"They [Nauru] want people to see the country in a more positive light rather than the punchline of a joke.

"So whether it's football, whether it's Aussie rules, whetherâ¯it'sâ¯rugby, basketball, cricket, weightlifting...â¯ just to be part of building a healthier Nauru is enough.

"But being a football lover, the best way I know how to have an impact is through football."

And the Briton, who is originally from Stevenage and worked at his hometown club when they were still in non-league, has a track history to prove it.

He previously set up a charity in the Cambodian city of Siem Reap which ended up turning into a professional academy that has so far produced 47 players who have progressed to play professionally in the Asian country, and is also running successful programmes in India bringing football to underserved communities.

All of his projects pose different challenges. One of the first challenges in Nauru is getting some footballs on to the island.

The volunteers have launched a campaign to give every child aged four to 14 a ball â roughly 2,000 children â and are working with churches and the island's 11 schools to deliver them. The balls will get delivered 200 at a time by plane to help manage the distribution and avoid potential waste.

Past attempts to introduce football to Nauru have focused on one-off fixtures, including two years ago when former Premier League striker Dave Kitson was appointed to lead a group of 18 Nauruans into a game after a two-week training camp.

Their opponents were set to be a Sunday league team from Reading called XL FC who use football as a way to achieve a healthier lifestyle. That match never happened for financial reasons and so the wait for that inaugural game goes on.

But the ethos has since changed and Nauru Soccer are looking longer term.

"Dave Kitson would have gone, I would have gone, and it would have been great for a couple of months, but it's a lot of money," says Pomroy, who has worked in football in every continent bar South America and Antarctica.

"Let'sâ¯start a culture on this island of football orâ¯sport andâ¯help it grow, because it's an important thing. Let's build the ecosystem, not just one-off games.

"My personal dream is that Nauru's first ever international game isâ¯played with all kids that areâ¯18 years old that had been coming through our system.

"So, say we found a group ofâ¯14-year-olds now and we said, 'Right,â¯let'sâ¯work with this group over the next three or four years'.

"And by the time they'reâ¯17-18â¯years old, that will be Nauru's first ever national team game."

Once Pomroy arrives for a training camp in December, he will set up coaching programmes for players and aspiring coaches so the sport can continue throughout the year.

A lot of this hinges on being able to find places to play.

Much of the land is privately owned or uninhabitable, but volunteer Tyrone Deiye is hoping to use some of his family's land to create more pitches than the sole one that currently exists - a dusty surface of phosphateâ¯over crushed dirt. He also says playing on indoor pitches may be an option.

Pomroy is keen to stress that Nauru Soccer is not trying to "force football down everyone's throat" but says it's about laying a foundation for a sport, promoting healthy lifestyles and building communities.

"The life lessons that you learn through football aren't just on the pitch, not just about winning and losing," says Pomroy, who manages this project while coaching in India.

"It's the friends that you make. It is learning to be humble. It's learning to look after your body. It's learning to get up when youâ¯fall down.

"And that's how I've seen it change people across the world. That's the dream for Nauru.

"If we sat here in five years' time, I genuinely believe that we will have a senior team that will be filled with 18, 19,â¯20-year-olds.

"Then in 20â¯years' time, someone from Nauru comes up to me and says, 'my life changed through football and the development programme'... That would be the ultimate dream."

Other Pacific island nations play football and expats from these countries sometimes play on Nauru, although Deiye says Nauruans "watch the expats play but they sort of laugh at them because they don't understand the game, they think it's funny".

"A lot of the other Pacific islands have got really good football teams and it makes those guys really happy," adds Deiye, who balances work as an urban planner in Nauru alongside his football work. "Those countries, they're really big into football. I want Nauru to be like that."

Last year, the Marshall Islands played the US Virgin Islands in their first international match. The Pacific island had been the self-proclaimed last nation on earth without a football team, but Nauru have also been claiming this tag.

There was also confusion in the middle of the Covid pandemic when a fake domestic league in Nauru was announced, with the hoax being very detailed down to team names and registered players.

But the Nauru Soccer Federation now has a real website, where it outlines its plans and also sells a national team shirt to raise funds to grow the game. Its main source of money for the project is through fundraisers, but that can be difficult to organise as the volunteers are also balancing full-time work and different time zones.

Even communication between the project's team members can be tricky â sometimes Deiye will not be contactable for a couple of days, only to come back to say that a storm had wiped out the internet on the island.

"This project's not short of challenges, for sure," says Pomroy.

"I think from what I can understand, Nauruans have been promised quite a lot throughout their history and been let down many times.

"Soâ¯their kind of attitude towards things tends to be 'we believe it when we see it' and they're very reluctant to get their hopes up.

"Butâ¯in general, the feedback we get is everyone is very, very excitedâ¯about it."

articles.summary: El estratega español aspira a seguir avanzando en Champions con 'su' Levski
articles.body: Julio Velázquez (Salamanca, 1981) puso fin la temporada pasada a la mayor dinastía en activo del planeta fútbol, las 14 Ligas consecutivas que acumulaba el Ludogorets. “No siento que sea mi mayor obra. En los 29 años que llevo entrenando he vivido grandes momentos”, reconocía a MARCA. El exentrenador de Poli Ejido, Villarreal, Murcia, Betis, Alcorcón, Alavés y Zaragoza, entre otros, condujo al Levski a poner fin a ¡17 años! de sequía en Bulgaria. 'Novias' no le han faltado, pero se ha mantenido fiel al banquillo del Georgi Asparuhov. “Recibí diferentes opciones en distintos contextos que podían resultar atractivas tanto a nivel deportivo como económico, pero tengo contrato y me siento querido y valorado. Soy feliz y, aunque ya se ha conseguido hacer historia, pienso que todavía se puede serguir construyendo. Eso es algo bonito y atractivo”, afirma el técnico español. Consiguió superar al Ludogorets a pesar de tener un presupuesto cinco veces inferior y confía en repetir con un español en sus filas: Álex Centelles ha llegado libre del Almería. “El mercado es muy dinámico y dura muchísimo. Al empezar a competir en Europa tan pronto tenemos que estar atentos a posibles entradas y salidas. Las diferencias a nivel presupuestario siguen existiendo, pero mi responsabilidad es sacar el máximo rendimiento en base a las herramientas que tenemos a nuestra disposición”, subraya. Su Levski superó ampliamente al Borac Banja Luka (1-5) en su estreno en Champions. Ahora le espera el Universitatea Craiova... pero la posibilidad de jugar la Fase de Grupos de la Liga de Campeones por primera vez desde la 2006-07 sigue pareciendo lejana. “El equipo compitió muy bien en la 1ª ronda previa. Ahora tenemos un rival muy duro y debemosofrecer nuestra mejor versión. El Levski lleva casi 20 años sin jugar una fase de grupos de una competición europea. El año pasado estuvimos cerquita de lograrlo. Si esta temporada lo logramos, en cualquiera de las tres competiciones, sería un exitazo”, reivindica Julio Velázquez. El triunfo ante el Universitatea Craiova tendría un valor añadido: “Si pasamos una ronda más, sí que nos garantizaríamos jugar, como mínimo, la Fase de Grupos de la Conference, lo que ya sería algo absolutamente extraordinario. Vamos día a día con el objetivo de seguir compitiendo en Champions: los chicos se lo han merecido”. Una cosa tiene clara: lo que funciona no se toca. “La temporada pasada conseguimos romper la hegemonía del Ludogorets gracias al gran trabajo de los jugadores e intentamos, en cualquier competición, mantenernos fieles a nuestra identidad. Es decir, ser un equipo muy proactivo con y sin balón. En Europa debemos ajustar detalles para sentirnos cómodos y competir de una manera fiable, pero intentamos llevarlo a cabo”, insiste Julio Velázquez, que podría rubricar un 'cuadro' de Champions.

articles.title: Kvaratskhelia se aferra a la 'vía Kevin Keegan' para soñar con el Balón de Oro
articles.standfirst: El inglés fue el último futbolista que ganó el galardón en año de Mundial sin participar en el torneo
articles.summary: El inglés fue el último futbolista que ganó el galardón en año de Mundial sin participar en el torneo
articles.body: ¿hasta qué punto debe influir el torneo más importante del fútbol en la elección del Balón de Oro? Históricamente, la Copa del Mundo ha servido para impulsar candidaturas, pero no ha sido una garantía de éxito. De hecho, la propia organización del premio ha querido recordarlo una vez concluido el Mundial de 2026. En un artículo publicado tras la final, el Balón de Oro recuerda que, aunque conquistar la Copa del Mundo ayuda, no garantiza el premio. De hecho, desde que el galardón se abrió a futbolistas de todo el mundo en 1995, sólo cuatro de los siete ganadores en años de Mundial fueron también campeones del mundo. La conclusión del propio artículo es todavía más reveladora: “Para ganar el Balón de Oro hay que haber sido el mejor jugador de la temporada, no solo del Mundial”. Ese criterio vuelve a situar en la conversación a futbolistas como Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, ausente del Mundial pero autor de una de las temporadas más completas del fútbol europeo. El georgiano firmó una campaña sobresaliente con el Paris Saint-Germain, registrando 19 goles y 10 asistencias en 48 partidos, consolidándose como uno de los grandes líderes del campeón de Europa. Su candidatura al Balón de Oro se construyó, sobre todo, en la Champions League, competición en la que terminó con 10 goles y seis asistencias en 16 encuentros y fue elegido 'Mejor Jugador de la Temporada' de la UEFA Champions League. Desde el 'playoff' de acceso a los octavos de final frente al Mónaco hasta la final participó directamente en 10 goles (seis tantos y cuatro asistencias). Además, en la final provocó el penalti que permitió al PSG igualar el encuentro antes de conquistar la primera Champions League de su historia. Y existe un precedente histórico que refuerza esa misma idea. En 1978, en pleno año de Mundial, Kevin Keegan conquistó el Balón de Oro después de una extraordinaria temporada con el Hamburgo, a pesar de que Inglaterra ni siquiera se había clasificado para la Copa del Mundo. Casi medio siglo después, la reflexión vuelve a ser la misma: si el Balón de Oro debe reconocer al mejor futbolista de toda la temporada, y no únicamente al más brillante del Mundial, la candidatura de Khvicha Kvaratskhelia mantiene argumentos más que suficientes para seguir entre las grandes favoritas al galardón.

articles.title: Yaya Touré, un estreno de Champions: "Los jugadores son las estrellas"
articles.standfirst: El exjugador del Barcelona debutó como entrenador del Slovan Bratislava en la previa
articles.summary: El exjugador del Barcelona debutó como entrenador del Slovan Bratislava en la previa
articles.body: Yaya Touré (Bouaké, 1983) llevaba tiempo preparándose para dar el salto a los banquillos. Ejerció de asistente en Olimpik Donetsk, Akhmat Grozny y Standard antes de convertirse en la 'mano derecha' de Roberto Mancini en Arabia Saudí.   Ahora, tras hacer sus 'pinitos' en la Academia del Tottenham, afronta su primera aventura en solitario como entrenador del Slovan Bratislava. "Mi objetivo era traer a una persona y una personalidad que haya vivido el mejor fútbol del mundo. Me causó una impresión maravillosa: tiene un gran deseo y motivación para triunfar como entrenador", reconocía Ivan Kmotrík Jr., director general del club.  "He tenido la oportunidad de trabajar con entrenadores excelentes en el pasado, pero anhelaba crear mi propio proyecto. Tengo mucho que aprender. Soy consciente de mis limitaciones", apunta el marfileño, que ha 'pasó por las manos' de Guardiola, Pellegrini, Mancini, Rijkaard... El ex de Barcelona, Manchester City, Mónaco y Olympiacos, entre otros, 'aparca' los más de 700 partidos, 127 goles, 73 asistencias y 18 títulos que coleccionó a lo largo de su carrera como jugador: "Lo tengo claro. Los jugadores son las estrellas. Están en el campo y han ganado las últimas ocho Ligas de forma consecutiva; es a los que todos miran".  La propuesta, eso sí, es innegociable. "Quiero que dominemos el juego y seamos agresivos cuando no tengamos la posesión. Nuestro principal objetivo debe ser marcar goles. No soy el tipo de entrenador que se toma los partidos con cautela: soy un ganador y me encanta ganar", confesaba a 'Dennik Sport'. Su estreno oficial llegó a lo grande, en Champions. El Slovan Bratislava de Yaya Touré -su hermano Kolo fue ayudante de Guardiola en el Manchester City- debutó con victoria sobre el Iberia 1999 (0-2) en la ida de la segunda ronda previa. "La actitud de los jugadores fue excelente. Estoy satisfecho, trabajamos bien, pero todavía tenemos margen de mejora. Hay que entender que este es un proceso que llevará tiempo. Estamos cambiando gradualmente la forma y la filosofía de juego, pero ya estamos viendo cosas buenas", afirma. Aún queda la vuelta y otras dos previas por delante, pero la Champions -ya la ganó con el Barcelona en 2009- le espera.

articles.title: Jurgen Klopp: Germany appoint former Liverpool boss as new head coach to replace Julian Nagelsmann
articles.summary: Jurgen Klopp returns to management as the new Germany head coach; Klopp left Liverpool in 2024 because he was "running out of energy", having won six trophies at the club in nine years; the 59-year-old had been working as Red Bull's global head of football; Klopp succeeds Julian Nagelsmann
articles.body:
Klopp has returned to management on a contract that runs until the end of the 2030 World Cup after leaving Liverpool in 2024 because he was "running out of energy" , having won six trophies in nine years at the club.

The 59-year-old was unveiled on Friday and issued a stark warning to journalists after his predecessor Julian Nagelsmann faced intense scrutiny and criticism from the media.

"It is my mission to make the national team squad a better team and hope the pool for me to choose from will be bigger, but it is not something I am doing against you, I am doing it for you. It is an honour," he said.

"I will be remunerated very graciously and if tomorrow Jurgen Klopp is s***, I will be gone. But if the DFB says let us discontinue the job, then that's it. And if you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace, I'll be gone. I'll just turn away. I know there are other countries where national team head coaches are treated even worse. I love this job but I am also ready to call it quits if needs be.

"Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any 'career' after the national team. This is the pinnacle, the high point of my footballing career as a coach. I will give everything I've got, and I have the best possible assistant coaching team."

Klopp was the first person the DFB turned to when Nagelsmann resigned after a disappointing World Cup ended with a penalty shoot-out exit to Paraguay in the last 32.

But Klopp has also warned his appointment won't guarantee success and that expectations need to be adjusted.

"Jurgen Klopp being in the job doesn't automatically mean we're going to be world champions," he said.

"Success is performance vs expectations. We need a new set of expectations. Many people have asked themselves, are we as good as France? If the answer is no, then that is not necessarily true. If the question is, do we have players like Dembele, Barcola, Mbappe? Then the answer is no, we don't, but we can still beat them.

"We don't want to play like Argentina, Spain, England or France. We want to play like Germany, do it the German way but very intense. Are we the number one team at the moment? No, we aren't; I accept that. Would we be happy to be the number two team? Then people would say we aren't number one.

"At the moment, we have 11 teams ahead of us. Yes, we can beat them, but for this to happen, you need to play very good, intense football."

His first game in charge is against the Netherlands in the Nations League on September 24.

Klopp won the Champions League, Premier League, Club World Cup, FA Cup and League Cup twice at Liverpool.

After a six-month break, Klopp was appointed head of global soccer at Red Bull and later stated that he had no desire to return to club management.

Klopp's former Liverpool assistants Pep Lijnders, who recently left Manchester City after Pep Guardiola's departure, and Peter Krawietz are part of the coaching staff, along with Sven Bender, who played under the German at Borussia Dortmund.

Per Mertesacker, who stepped down as Arsenal's academy manager after eight years at the end of last season, will become Germany's sporting director in January, replacing Andreas Rettig.

'Klopp is the perfect manager at the right time - and he wants to make changes'

Sky Germany's Patrick Berger speaking on Sky Sports News:

"For Klopp, it's very important to make some things different to the former coach of the German national team, Julian Nagelsmann. He wants to have a direct relationship to the players, he wants to see them directly in the stadiums.

"This was something Nagelsmann was criticised for in the past because he didn't see or visit Kevin Schade at Brentford, he didn't visit Yann Aurel Bisseck at Inter, he didn't visit Niclas Fullkrug at West Ham. This is a point Klopp wants to change. He wants to bring all the people in Germany behind him.

"He has a list of around 57 to 60 players, he said, that he finds very attractive. The kind of players who have the chance in future to play for Germany. He said every player who is able to wear the Germany shirt should be aware that he may be calling.

"The German public have reacted very well because he's the perfect manager, he's here at the right time and is someone who has the credibility, the energy after two years out of being in this daily job as a head coach. We are a proud football nation and this makes the people in Germany believe we can be successful again in the future."

articles.standfirst: El atacante del Barça reconoce que ha necesitado ayuda y que su coach personal ha tenido trabajo extra para ayudarle a salir adelante
articles.summary: El atacante del Barça reconoce que ha necesitado ayuda y que su coach personal ha tenido trabajo extra para ayudarle a salir adelante
articles.body: "Ha sido el peor verano de mi vida. Estaba en el mejor momento, todo salía bien y llegó la lesión. También se aprende de estas situaciones, pero es cierto que este verano lo he pasado muy mal.   He salido adelante gracias a mi familia, mi compañera y mis amigos. He necesitado ayuda. Ya tenía antes, pero mi coach me ha ayudado mucho a salir adelante", las palabras de Fermín en el programa a Tot Costa de Catalunya Ràdio desde el stage de pretemporada del Barça en Inglaterra son definitorias.  Fermín reconoce en la entrevista que los primeros partidos de España se los tuvo que ahorrar. "Los primeros partidos de la selección española en el Mundial no los vi. No podía. Quería estar allí en el Mundial. Que quede claro que me ha hecho muy feliz ver a mis compañeros ganar el Mundial. En el tramo final del Mundial ya lo pasé algo mejor y decidí ir a ver la final en directo a Nueva York". "Me encuentro cada día mejor. No tengo molestias, que es importante. Si todo va bien, en el Gámper podría jugar ya unos minutos. La intención es volver de esa lesión con más motivación. Creo que estoy muy preparado. Ya he demostrado cómo puedo ayudar al Barça y esta próxima temporada tengo que seguir igual". "El sueño de la Champions es compartido con todo el equipo. Los dos últimos años hemos estado cerca. Esta temporada puede ser buena. Llevamos tres años jugando juntos y hemos vivido muchas cosas. Siento que estamos preparados para ganar la Champions. Ganar la tercera liga consecutiva es difícil. Será un año complicado. Pero si nosotros estamos centrados en nuestro juego y estamos unidos podemos ganar la tercera liga".
