articles.title: Josep Martínez: "El accidente fue una tragedia, dolió mucho y con razón"
articles.standfirst: El portero español será el titular durante la próxima temporada con el Inter de Milan
articles.summary: El portero español será el titular durante la próxima temporada con el Inter de Milan
articles.body: Hay tragedias que te marcan de por vida. Que son díficiles de superar y, aunque el tiempo sana, no se olvidan. Es el caso de Josep Martínez, portero español del Inter de Milan, que en una entrevista para la Gazzetta, ha hablado de ciertos temas de relevancia. Especial énfasis en el accidente en el que se vió envuelto en 2025, cuando atropelló a Paolo Saibane, de 81 años, y le costó la vida. Un momento que marcó un antes y un después en su vida. Un impacto que le costó mucho procesar: "Conté con el apoyo de mis compañeros, mi familia y mis amigos. Un profesional también me brindó su ayuda. Pero no hay secretos: cuando ocurre una tragedia como esta, duele, y con razón. Fue un momento difícil. Luego, con el tiempo, logré superarlo", afirmó el español de 28 años. Martínez será el portero titular del Inter durante esta próxima campaña. La venta de Sommer le ha dado vía libre para ocuparse de la portería, después de dos temporadas como suplente: "Cuando no estás jugando, tu mente es fundamental. Siempre me he centrado en prepararme bien, esperando el momento oportuno. El fútbol es así: ahora tengo esta oportunidad y quiero aprovecharla al máximo." El recuerdo del accidente pesó mucho en su evolución como portero. Una carga que provocó un bajón notable en su fuerza mental: "Ocurrió algo fuera del campo que me impidió trabajar como me hubiera gustado. Un futbolista necesita tener la mente despejada para rendir al máximo. Por suerte, ahora puedo dejar todo atrás y centrarme en la nueva temporada, sin pensar en lo sucedido. Tengo muchas ganas de jugar, confirmó de forma rotunda Martínez. A pesar de sus problemas, su fuerza de voluntad siempre le ayudó a llegar al momento en el que se encuentra ahora: "Yo también creía que merecía jugar, porque me sentía preparado. Pero esto no solo aplica al segundo portero, sino a todos los integrantes del equipo. Es cierto que los suplentes competitivos ayudan a los titulares a entrenar mejor y a mantenerse en plena forma." El Inter ha cerrado la incorporación de otro portero, aunque de perfil veterano y con experiencia para el vestuario, Provedel: "Es un buen tipo, muy humilde, y tratará de complicarle las cosas al entrenador. Es normal. Yo intentaré hacer mi parte", respondió de forma cercana sobre su nuevo compañero en la portería del Inter. El guardameta lo tiene claro, este Inter tiene equipo para pelear por todo: "No nos rendimos ante nada. Tenemos que ser ambiciosos en todos los frentes, incluso en la Champions League: queremos intentar llegar hasta el final otra vez", contestó con ambición Josep Martínez. También, con Luis de la Fuente en mente y una posible convocatoria con España: "Sería un sueño. Si logro consolidarme en el Inter, tendré una oportunidad, ¿por qué no? Pero los porteros españoles son increíbles. Los mejores del mundo, junto con Donnarumma, a quien nos enfrentamos en Hong Kong."

articles.title: El Bodo/Glimt vuelve a la carga: "La Champions supuso un nivel completamente nuevo para nosotros"
articles.standfirst: Ganaron a City, Atlético, Inter... y ahora se miden al Union Saint-Gilloise en la 3ª ronda previa
articles.summary: Ganaron a City, Atlético, Inter... y ahora se miden al Union Saint-Gilloise en la 3ª ronda previa
articles.body: Cinco victorias consecutivas frente a Manchester City (3-1), Atlético (1-2), Inter (3-1 y 1-2) y Sporting CP (3-0) convirtieron al Bodo/Glimt en el equipo revelación de la pasada Champions League. Pasaron de tener un 99,7% de opciones de caer eliminados en la Fase Liga a erigirse en el primer equipo noruego que superaba una eliminatoria en Liga de Campeones. Es más, rozaron los cuartos... pero acabaron sucumbiendo en la prórroga ante el Sporting (5-0). “La Champions supuso un nivel completamente nuevo para nosotros. Nos llevó un tiempo adaptarnos, pero aprendimos rápido. Todo nuestro recorrido ha consistido en desarrollar un mayor nivel de competitividad. La derrota ante el Sporting fue una gran decepción, pero también hubo muchas lecciones valiosas que esperamos nos hagan más fuertes”, asegura Havard Sakariassen, director deportivo del Bodo/Glimt, a MARCA. Ahora vuelven a la carga. Les espera un rival duro, el Union Saint-Gilloise, en la 3ª ronda previa. Deberían pasar otra más para volver a la Fase Liga de la Champions. “Veremos qué pasa, pero nos hemos preparado bien para volver a competir en Europa. Aprovecharemos todo lo que hemos aprendido y esperamos añadir algunos pilares más a lo que el Bodø/Glimt está construyendo”, subraya Sakariassen. El director deportivo del Bodo tiene mérito. Se ha ido Kasper Hogh (Celtic), pero ha logrado retener a Berg, Hauge, Knutsen... “No siempre el césped es más verde al otro lado. Aquí los jugadores y los entrenadores tienen la oportunidad de desarrollarse, al tiempo que logran grandes cosas”, insiste. Vuelven con las energías renovadas por el parón mundialista. Desde marzo de 2024 habían disputado 116 partidos oficiales sin un mes consecutivo de descanso entre medias: “Ha sido estupendo para todos tener la oportunidad de realizar una pretemporada adecuada. Nos espera un otoño exigente, pero emocionante”. Un sobresfuerzo que les privó de ganar su tercera Liga consecutiva: “Estábamos al límite en lo que respecta a la carga de trabajo. Aún así, rendimos a un nivel muy alto”. Este curso, después de 16 jornadas, son líderes: “Nuestra ambición es mejorar día a día y sacar todo el potencial que se puede lograr dirigiendo a un club de fútbol como el Bodø/Glimt”.

articles.title: Sorteo 'playoffs' de la Champions: el Celtic se jugará contra el LASK el billete a la fase Liga
articles.standfirst: En juego las últimas plazas para estar el 27 de agosto en la composición del Top 36
articles.summary: En juego las últimas plazas para estar el 27 de agosto en la composición del Top 36
articles.body: La eliminatoria Celtic-LASK y los enfrentamientos de los ganadores de la tercera ronda previa Olympiacos-NEC Nimega y Union SG-Bodo Glimt sobresalen en los playoffs de clasificación para la Liga de Campeones 2026-27, según el sorteo celebrado este lunes en la sede de la UEFA en Nyon. Los encuentros se disputarán los días 18 y 19 (ida) y 25 y 26 (vuelta). Los vencedores accederán a la fase Liga del máximo torneo continental. El conjunto escocés tratará de no fallar ante un LASK que intenta hacer historia. Mientras, Olympiacos se mide ante el NEC neerlandés para volver a la fase de Liga, en la que la pasada campaña tuvieron un buen papel el Union Saint Gilloise belga y el Bodo Glimt, sobre todo el cuadro noruego, que llegó a los octavos de final, en los que cayó tras la prórroga ante el Sporting Portugal. También avecina una eliminatoria el duelo que medirá a los ganadores de las eliminatorias Fenerbahce/Sturm Graz y Sparta Praga/Lyon. articles.title: Premier League summer transfer window: What your club still needs to do in the week before Deadline Day
articles.summary: We are entering the final week of the Premier League transfer window and nearly every club is still active in the market ahead of the Tuesday September 1 deadline; Follow every twist and turn with our dedicated Transfer Centre blog and on Sky Sports News
articles.body:
Arsenal will not give up on the signing of Julian Alvarez right until the end but, with his heart set on a move to Barcelona and Atletico refusing to sell to them, it still looks unlikely to happen at this stage.

Everyone is waiting to see if Alvarez changes his stance and opens up to the idea, but if he doesn't, Arsenal are happy with their squad and won't just pivot to any other forward. They want top quality only.

Meanwhile, Al Hilal are trying to sign Gabriel Martinelli and the player is understood to be seriously considering a move to Saudi. Ethan Nwaneri could depart on loan while Arsenal are understood to be willing to listen to offers for Gabriel Jesus.

Mikel Arteta has ruled out the possibility of Myles Lewis-Skelly or Martin Zubimendi leaving.

Aston Villa face a busy final week with more potential ins and outs in a summer of upheaval. They are working on forward options, a new midfielder and a replacement for Ezri Konsa at the back. Most recently, they have made approaches for forwards Jean Philippe Mateta and Raphael Leao and have been in talks for defenders Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Joel Ordonez.

With Amadou Onana out and now new signing Joao Gomes suspended, Villa are close to signing free agent Leon Goretzka to strengthen the midfield.

Up front, Nicolas Jackson at Chelsea is also another option if they lose Ollie Watkins to Al Hilal.

Emi Martinez's future is still uncertain after Villa signed Zion Suzuki in goal before the Argentina star had found another club to go to.

Bournemouth are expecting the signing of Juventus goalkeeper Michele Di Gregorio to be their final transfer of the summer. He has joined on a season-long loan which includes an option to buy at £12m.

As ever, Bournemouth are still open to a market opportunity should one arise in the final days of the window.

There is a possibility that their resolve is tested by a big bid for Alex Scott from one of either Chelsea or Manchester City, depending on what happens with Enzo Fernandez's future.

However, Bournemouth do not want to sell and insist they are under no pressure to do so. The midfielder has two years left on his current deal but has turned down the club's offer of a new one.

Brentford are very happy with their squad and rightly so; they took Spurs to task on the opening day with a resounding 3-0 win.

The only area of the side they are still looking at is on the left, but only if they can be assured to add more quality; ergo market opportunities only. There is some flexibility on the profile too; it could be a left-back or left-winger.

They have been keen on West Ham's El Hadji Malick Diouf, who is primarily a left-back, which would allow Keane Lewis-Potter to operate further forward more regularly. But he is one of four left-back options at the club including Rico Henry, Jayden Meghoma and Aaron Hickey, so they are not desperate.

Meghoma could be one of several who go on loan.

Brighton have work to do with Yankuba Minteh attracting strong interest from Liverpool and Carlos Baleba joining Manchester United.

They are working on a deal for BSC Young Boys left-back Jaouen Hadjam with Maxim De Cuyper starting the season playing further forward.

Brighton are also exploring a potential deal for Deportivo La Coruna winger Yeremay Hernandez but face competition from Hull City among others.

They could also sign another midfielder, with Baleba - and potentially Matt O'Riley - leaving. O'Reilly has interest from Lyon and other top European clubs having recovered from an illness.

Brighton would consider offers for Evan Ferguson and Igor Julio if they arrive.

The only first-team position that could see a change in is midfield. Manchester City are interested in Enzo Fernandez and, if he leaves, Alex Scott and Adam Wharton are among the players Chelsea are expected to have a serious look at. The remaining business will be all outgoings, with as many as nine players leaving Stamford Bridge. Aston Villa are expected to move for Nicolas Jackson if Ollie Watkins goes to Al Hilal, while Liam Delap is edging closer to joining Nottingham Forest.

Chelsea no longer see Leeds as a loan destination for Mykhailo Mudryk, amid interest from sister club Strasbourg, while Hull want Dario Essugo but Strasbourg could also be a destination for the young midfielder.

Tosin has multiple interest from abroad and fellow centre-back Axel Disasi is close to signing for Crystal Palace.

Coventry are hoping to wrap up their summer business with two more signings before they are next in Premier League action against fellow promoted side Hull City on Saturday.

They want to bring in a left-back and a centre-back before the deadline, having already added 10 players to Frank Lampard's squad in the hope of securing Premier League survival.

Coventry have already agreed a deal with Brentford to sign Ethan Pinnock. The centre-back is expected to have a medical this week ahead of completing a transfer understood to be worth up to £6m.

Crystal Palace are set to complete the signing of Axel Disasi on loan from Chelsea as a replacement for Maxence Lacroix but are yet to find a successor to Marc Guehi and could sign another centre-back. Palace have been exploring options to reinforce out wide. Free agent Solly March is one they have been working towards after his Brighton exit. There are question marks over three of Palace's most key players, Daniel Munoz, Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr, in the final week.

Sarr has reported interest from Galatasaray, but suggestions the winger is refusing to train are wide of the mark. He is currently injured.

Aston Villa have made an approach for Mateta, who has entered the final year of his deal. He was close to leaving six months ago for AC Milan. Munoz has interest from a number of clubs, including Everton.

David Moyes still wants a right-back and a potential change among his centre-forwards, as well as maybe another winger.

He wants Strasbourg's Guela Doue but the price is prohibitive, while others he likes are RB Leipzig's Ridle Baku and Crystal Palace's Daniel Munoz.

Everton face a similar situation with Liam Delap, but Nottingham Forest are currently ahead of them in the race to sign the Chelsea striker. Beto has interest from Fiorentina so it remains to be seen if some movement happens there.

There is still a chance Jack Grealish returns after his loan spell last season but he was in Manchester City's squad at the weekend as they try to get more bodies in themselves.

Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa has said he wants more business to be done as he looks to bring balance to his squad. They seem to be prioritising a new right-back at the moment while they are yet to replace Harry Wilson and Issa Diop with a new winger or centre-back.

Talks have been held with Rennes over a deal for 20-year-old Morocco international centre-back Abdelhamid Ait-Boudlal but the French club appear reluctant to sell.

Summer signing Gonzalo Garcia appears to be Arbeloa's favoured striker, so will the returning Rodrigo Muniz be happy with that, or does there need to be a change among the back-up strikers? Let's see.

Hull City are expecting to be busy in the final week of the window and are looking to bring in at least five more players before the deadline.

The promoted side are close to reaching an agreement to sign centre-forward Ilyas Ansah from Union Berlin and they are in talks with Deportivo La Coruna for winger Yeremay Hernandez.

Hull are also putting the finishing touches to an agreement with Nice for forward Mohamed-Ali Cho in a deal worth in the region of £15m and are still in the race to sign Stoke winger Sorba Thomas. Meanwhile, they have an interest in Chelsea midfielder Dario Essugo, too.

Several squad players could leave the MKM Stadium before September 1.

Ipswich remain in talks with Bayer Leverkusen over a deal for midfielder Exequiel Palacios, after a bid was rejected last week.

They are looking to strengthen further in attack and midfield, with options also being explored for more depth at centre-forward. Ipswich are thought to be one of the clubs who like Burnley's Zian Flemming.

Sheffield Wednesday have agreed a straight loan deal with Ipswich to sign striker Ali Al-Hamadi. He is one of several players that could leave before the deadline and could mean another forward option is brought into Portman Road. Wrexham are in talks to sign Anis Mehmeti, while Chiedozie Ogbene, Cameron Humphreys and Alex Palmer also have interest from elsewhere.

Leeds will only do more if they can genuinely improve Daniel Farke's squad.

Checks have been made on Conrad Harder's availability at RB Leipzig, but club sources are playing down the chances of adding a striker.

Their strong interest in Mykhailo Mudryk remains despite doubts around Chelsea's willingness to do a deal with Leeds amid interest from Strasbourg.

Gabriel Gudmundsson's injury has highlighted the need for Leeds to sign full-back cover. As things stand, that also looks difficult to do.

Leeds are lining up Eintracht Frankfurt's Michael Zetterer to be the back-up goalkeeper, but a deal cannot proceed until Frankfurt land a new No 1. If Zetterer comes in, Lucas Perri can go to Torino.

Meanwhile, Mateo Joseph and Largie Ramazani are searching for new clubs.

Liverpool's priority, as it has been throughout the summer, is still to reinforce in wide areas.

They have been pursuing PSG duo Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye, while Brighton have also rejected two Liverpool offers for Yankuba Minteh, the latest being £60m.

PSG's valuation of £145m has been a stumbling block but Liverpool are currently the only club chasing the forward, who has entered the final two years of his deal and has grown dissatisfied with his role in the team.

Liverpool do not want to sell Cody Gakpo amid interest from Tottenham and Manchester City and would likely need two new wingers in before considering letting the Dutchman go.

Manchester City look like being one of the busiest clubs, in and out. Savio has joined Tottenham and Omar Marmoush is likely to follow if City can get bodies in the door. Palmeiras winger Allan is on his way over, while they also like Spurs target Cody Gakpo at Liverpool. With another midfielder in Nico Gonzalez getting closer to Newcastle, City will sign a replacement and are interested in Enzo Fernandez, Alex Scott and Manu Kone.

City have been after a back-up striker all summer with interest in Junior Kroupi, but he is out injured until around October.

Manchester United are still on the search for a left-back but will only act if the right player becomes available. It is possible Carlos Baleba could be the club's last signing of the window. As it stands, potential deals for Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly look unlikely. Alejandro Balde has been mooted as an option with Barcelona willing to let him go. United are aware of his situation but have not actively been pursuing him. United could wait until next summer to pursue their defensive targets rather than look for a stopgap option as they did with the midfield a year ago. Further incomings are unlikely. Interest from Italy for Joshua Zirkzee has not progressed and he is currently likely to stay, as is Marcus Rashford, who was given the club's No 9 shirt for the season.

Newcastle are working on potentially signing a midfielder, wide forward and a striker before the window closes.

A deal to sign Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City is understood to be advancing and there is hope an agreement can be struck this week with head coach Matthias Jaissle keen to add experience in the midfield.

Joe Willock's impressive performance in the 2-2 draw against Liverpool could see him stay at Newcastle in this window despite strong interest from Besiktas.

Nick Pope could depart with his replacements already through the door, while Jacob Murphy also has interest from Everton.

Nottingham Forest are working hard to bring in Liam Delap from Chelsea to improve their striking options following Taiwo Awoniyi's £9m move to Coventry.

They have been pursuing Lucas Bergvall as an Elliot Anderson replacement, but Roberto De Zerbi insists he is staying at Spurs.

Forest could also add a right wing-back with Dodo at Fiorentina a player of interest.

Dilane Bakwa is set to join Lille on loan, while centre-backs Zach Abbott and Tyler Bindon could also depart on temporary moves amid interest from Watford.

Sunderland are expected to be busy and could bring in three more signings with a centre-back, winger and striker on the agenda. They are keen on Sporting winger Geny Catamo, but that would likely be an expensive deal to do. Jason Seelt is likely to go out on loan once a new contract is agreed. Udinese have been in contact with Sunderland, while Monza are also keen along with clubs in the Championship and Bundesliga.

Tottenham have spent north of £300m but still hope to sign two more forward players. Spurs are close to agreeing a deal to sign Omar Marmoush from Man City and are also interested in Liverpool's Cody Gakpo. Pedro Neto is an alternative target but he is valued at close to £100m by Chelsea. Spurs could see Pape Matar Sarr and Richarlison depart before the window closes, while Lucas Bergvall is now expected to stay at Spurs, according to Roberto De Zerbi.

articles.title: Sergi Domínguez, la 'muralla' del Dinamo: "Pensé en Dani Olmo porque mi sueño es volver al Barcelona"
articles.standfirst: Debutó con Flick, levantó Liga y Copa en Croacia y ahora sueña con disputar la Champions
articles.summary: Debutó con Flick, levantó Liga y Copa en Croacia y ahora sueña con disputar la Champions
articles.body: Sergi Domínguez (Barcelona, 2005) escaló junto a Lamine y Cubarsí a través de las categorías inferiores del Barça. Llegó a debutar con el primer equipo a las órdenes de Flick en 2024, pero prefirió seguir la vía Dani Olmo. El pasado verano fichó por el Dinamo Zagreb con el sueño de, algún día, regresar a casa. Pregunta. ¿Cómo termina Sergi Domínguez en el Dinamo Zagreb el pasado verano? Respuesta. Acabé la temporada con el Barça y la idea era que salir cedido o vendido, pero en ningún momento me imaginaba que acabaría en Croacia. Creía que jugaría en Segunda división en España. Sin embargo, a mitad de junio me llamó Albert Capellas, que había sido coordinador de la cantera del Barcelona, y me preguntó si estaba interesado en venir. Hablamos, me comentó que el Dinamo había cambiado de filosofía y me gustó la idea. Fue, principalmente, gracias a que Capellas [ahora director de la escuela de Fútbol del Dinamo] ya me conocía.    P. ¿Qué es lo que terminó de convencerle? R.De las opciones que tenía era la mejor. Aún era pronto, pero creo que no iba a tener ninguna opción mejor. Suponía dar el salto al fútbol profesional al 100% y que teníamos asegurados ocho partidos en la Europa League. Eso también sumó mucho la verdad. P. ¿Influyó mucho el paso de Dani Olmo por el Dinamo?  R. Sí, sí que lo pensé. De hecho, hablé con él antes de venir. Dani vino aquí, luego se fue al Leipzig y después volvió al Barcelona. Por eso pensé en él porque, al final, mi sueño, es volver a jugar en casa otra vez.  Vi que a él le fue bien y que había otros muchos jugadores, ya no españoles, también croatas, que habían dado el saltos a grandes clubes siendo jóvenes desde el Dinamo. Eso también tuvo bastante peso. P. Dani Olmo llegó a hablar croata. ¿Lo domina? R. Estudio croata y del fútbol entiendo más o menos, diría un 70% de lo que se habla. Fuera del campo, si voy a comprar o a un restaurante, puedo hablar, pero seguir una conversación rutinaria es muy difícil. Las palabras no guardan similitudes ni con el español, ni con el catalán, ni con el inglés. Y eso lo complica bastante. De todos modos, lo estudio por las tardes y así ocupo parte de mi tiempo libre. P. Para quién aún no le conozca, ¿cómo se definiría como futbolista? R. Me considero un jugador con buena salida. Soy tranquilo con balón y agresivo sin él. P. Diversas estadísticas del CIES a lo largo de la temporada pasada le situaron como el cuarto central sub 21 con más aceleraciones por 90' (6,02) dentro de las 38 principales Ligas de Europa, el quinto con más pases progresivos (7,94) y el octavo con más porcentaje de éxito en duelos a ras de suelo (73,2%). Era, también, el séptimo sub 23 con mayor porcentaje de duelos áereos ganados (75,9%).  R. Estar entre los mejores centrales de Europa en distintos baremos es bueno. Intento ser lo más completo posible con y sin balón. Lo que necesitaba era jugar para poder demostrar mi valía y creo que, poco a poco, lo estoy consiguiendo. P. ¿Quiénes son sus ídolos? ¿En quién se fija? R. Cuando era niño me gustaban Piqué y Sergio Ramos. Pero, actualmente, mi jugador favorito es Van Dijk. P. Su primera temporada en Zagreb no pudo terminar mejor. Ganaron Liga y Copa. R. Para el Dinamo ganar Liga y Copa en Croacia es, hasta cierto punto, normal, pero venía de no ganar ninguna de las dos la tempora anterior. En lo personal ha sido un año en el que he aprendido mucho, jugando cada tres días. Para un futbolista eso es lo mejor. Ganas confianza y experiencia. Ganar como ganamos Copa y Liga, con 15 puntos de ventaja, es inmejorable, la verdad. P. En lo personal cerró el curso con 41 partidos (3.513'), dos goles y cuatro asistencias. No sólo eso. Entró en el 'Once Ideal' de la temporada en la Liga croata.  R. Sí. Entramos varios del Dinamo [ríe]. Me fue muy bien. Jugué mucho, que era lo que necesitaba después de salir del Barcelona.  P. ¿El Dinamo es muy distinto al Barcelona? R. No. El año pasado cambió la directiva y entraron Capellas y Boban, que es el presidente. La mentalidad de juego es muy parecida. Casi igual: 1-4-3-3, jugar el balón, presión alta... Obviamente hay diferencias en las instalaciones y en el presupuesto, pero es que el Barça es, en mi opinión, el mejor equipo de Europa.  P. ¿En qué siente que le ha hecho mejor su paso por el fútbol croata? R. En lo que no es tanto fútbol con balón. He ganado experiencia en los duelos, a nivel de agresividad, posicionamiento... Es una Liga más dura en ese aspecto. No es tan táctica ni técnica como la española. P. Debutó en Champions con el Barcelona. ¿Le hace ilusión jugarla con el Dinamo? R. Sí, obviamente. El objetivo a corto plazo es meternos a Champions. Jugar en Champions, de titular y siendo importante es muy diferente a jugar Europa League o cualquier otra competición. P. Vienen de superar al Thun, ahora les espera el Kauno Žalgiris y tendrían otra ronda por delante. ¿Cómo de lejos ve la Fase de Grupos? R. Ahora más cerca. Nos quedan cuatro partidos y creo que tenemos bastantes posibilidades. Confío en el equipo y en que clasificaremos. P. El Thun se lo puso difícil. Necesitaron ir a la prórroga. R. Sí, fue una eliminatoria bastante loca y bastante dura. Por suerte, pasamos.  P. ¿Le gustaría que le tocara algún español si llegan a Fase de Grupos? R. Me haría gracia, sobre todo, jugar contra el Barcelona. Sería enfrentarme a amigos míos y contra todos los miembros del 'staff' que conozco.  P. Dani Olmo le convenció de recalar en Zagreb. ¿A Dani Rodríguez le convenció usted de fichar por el Dinamo? R. Con Dani he jugado cinco años y tenemos muy buena relación. Cuando sonó en el mercado de invierno ya hablamos. Obviamente, le aconsejé venir. Creo que no hay mejor sitio para los jóvenes. Es una Liga muy competitiva y con mucha visibilidad. P. Además de Dani Rodríguez, comparte defensa con Raúl Torrente. ¿Cómo es la familia española del Dinamo? R. Nos llevamos muy bien, la verdad. Está también Matteo Pérez Vinlöf, que es sueco-peruano, y Scott McKenna, que aprendió español de su paso por Las Palmas. Somos varios y hemos formado un pequeño grupo en el que tenemos buenas conversaciones.   P. Compartió equipo con Lamine Yamal y Pau Cubarsí. ¿Sintió envidia sana al verles ganar el Mundial? R. No sólo de ellos, sentí envidia sana de todos los que se proclamaron campeones del mundo. Lo de Pau y Lamine no es normal. Es una locura. Cubarsí, con 19 año, fue uno de los mejores de España... y del Mundial. Lamine también ha tenido un papel importante. Cada vez que recibe parece que va a pasar algo.   P. ¿Ha tenido la oportunidad de felicitarles? R. Sí. Les escribí justo después del Mundial felicitándoles. Yo lo viví aquí en Croacia, pero metí un grito cuando marcó el gol Ferran...  P. A nivel selección, imagino que su objetivo es hacerse fuerte en la sub 21.  R. Ahora mismo estoy centrado en mi club. Si rindes a buen nivel y demuestras tu valía, la oportunidad de ir a la selección te llega. En cualquier caso, acudir con la selección, sea en un papel importante o no, es una buena noticia.   P. El Barcelona le vendió por 1,2 millones de euros y se reservó un porcentaje de una futura venta. ¿Le gustaría volver siguiendo los pasos de Dani Olmo? R. Sí. Mi objetivo final es volver a mi casa y jugar en el Barça. Ojalá se pueda. Es difícil, pero lo intentaré. Aún tengo tiempo. P. Este verano ha sonado para diversos equipos, sobre todo para la Lazio. ¿Por dónde pasa su futuro? R. No tengo ni idea. Yo no he hablado con nadie. Aunque hubiera una oferta importante, de mucho dinero, mi objetivo es clasificar al Dinamo para la Champions. Cuando lo logremos, ya veremos qué pasa. Pero, insisto, ahora el objetivo es meternos en Champions.

articles.title: Mendilibar salta al ruedo de la Champions: "Estamos listos"
articles.standfirst: Su Olympiacos se mide al NEC Nimega en la tercera ronda de clasificación y ya sabe su posible rival en la siguiente fase en caso de avanzar: Union SG o Bodo/Glimt
articles.summary: Su Olympiacos se mide al NEC Nimega en la tercera ronda de clasificación y ya sabe su posible rival en la siguiente fase en caso de avanzar: Union SG o Bodo/Glimt
articles.body: Acaba de arrancar el mes de agosto... pero la Champions League no se detiene. Una vez superadas las dos primeras rondas previas del torneo, ya comienzan a asomar la cabeza algunos 'cocos' que persiguen el objetivo de clasificar a la fase liga de 36 equipos. Uno de los más destacados es el Olympiacos de Mendilibar, que entra en esta tercera fase de la Liga de Campeones para medirse al sorprendente NEC Nimega, una de las grandes revelaciones de la temporada pasada en Europa tras alcanzar la final de la Copa de Países Bajos y finalizar en la tercera posición de la Eredivisie. "Es un equipo muy atrevido, como hemos visto en las temporadas anteriores y también en las etapas del entrenador (Dick Schreuder) cuando estaba en el Castellón", analizaba Mendilibar, que contará a sus órdenes con los fichajes de Stefan Ortega, Pablo Maffeo, David Carmo, Joel Roca o Jota Silva. Aún así, reconoce que todavía "pueden ocurrir muchas cosas" hasta el cierre del mercado. No será, ni mucho menos, una presa fácil para un Olympiacos que en la pasada edición llegó a 'colarse' en el 'playoff', donde cayó contra el Bayer Leverkusen. Ahora bien, en caso de pasar de ronda el panorama no es mucho más alentador en la siguiente fase, puesto que deberá medirse al ganador del Union Saint-Gilloise vs. Bodo/Glimt. Otros dos equipos que también disputaron la pasada edición de la Champions. El Olympiacos ya lleva cerca de un mes de pretemporada. Sin embargo, en el momento que han subido el nivel de exigencia de los amistosos las sensaciones no han sido positivas y han encadenado tres derrotas consecutivas contra Ajax (1-0), Amberes (3-0) y AZ (3-2). 'Mendi', en cualquier caso, considera que "la preparación y el trabajo han sido buenos" y esperan "demostrar estar listos" para afrontar la eliminatoria. Partidos de la tercera ronda previa de la Champions 26-27: Mendilibar no es el único técnico español que se juega su futuro en el torneo. Todavía continúa vivo el Levski Sofía de Julio Velázquez, que tras acabar con la tiranía del Ludogorets en Bulgaria quiere estar en la fase final del torneo. Ahora le toca enfrentarse al Kairat y, si supera la eliminatoria, espera el AEK de Atenas. No será una tarea ni mucho menos fácil. Para sorpresa, eso sí, la del Mjällby, equipo de la pequeña localidad —menos de 2.000 habitantes— de Hällevik, ubicada en el sur de Suecia, que se la juega con el Slovan Bratislava de Yayá Touré. El Dinamo de Zagreb, que cuenta en sus filas con Sergi Domínguez, Raúl Torrente y Dani Rodríguez, se enfrenta al Kauno Zalgiris; el Celje con el Ararat y el Estrella Roja frente al Be'er Sheva. La eliminatoria con menos 'pedigrí' la protagonizarán AGF y Sabah. En el horizonte, en un polo completamente opuesto, aguarda una eliminatoria de altura entre el Fenerbahçe de Asensio, que se medirá al Sturm Graz, y un Olympique de Lyon que se jugará el pase contra el Sparta Praga. Sobre el papel, ambos deberían seguir adelante. Pero, en caso de hacerlo, sólo uno podrá estar en el sorteo de la fase liga que tendrá lugar el próximo jueves 27 de agosto de 2026 en la sede de la UEFA en Nyon. La cosa empieza a ponerse seria.

articles.title: Euro 2016: Inside story of the summer that changed Welsh football
articles.summary: A decade on from Euro 2016, key figures tell BBC Sport Wales the inside story of the summer that changed Welsh football forever.
articles.body:
"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

articles.title: Mendilibar juega con fuego
articles.standfirst: Su Olympiacos no pasó del empate contra el NEC Nimega (0-0) y se jugará el pase a la última fase previa de la Champions en Países Bajos
articles.summary: Su Olympiacos no pasó del empate contra el NEC Nimega (0-0) y se jugará el pase a la última fase previa de la Champions en Países Bajos
articles.body: Mendilibar y su Olympiacos quieren estar presentes en el sorteo de la fase liga de la Champions 26-27 que tendrá lugar el próximo 27 de agosto en Nyon. Ahora bien, el ex de Eibar o Sevilla ya advirtió que el NEC Nimega no se lo pondría fácil... y no fueron capaces de pasar del empate en Grecia (0-0). Dani García, ex del Eibar y Athletic presente en la sala de máquinas junto al talentoso Mouzakitis, no fue el único futbolista español que formó de inicio en Olympiacos. Joel Roca, incorporado este mismo mercado desde el Girona, partió desde la banda por delante de Gelson Martins o Jota Silva. Maffeo, por su parte, esperó su oportunidad en el banquillo. El ambiente en El Pireo, como de costumbre, era ensordecedor. Una auténtica olla a presión de la que trató de aprovecharse un Olympiacos que, desde el pitido inicial, se instaló en campo rival e imponer un ritmo alto. Le costaba expandirse al NEC Nimega. Ahora bien, no renunció a su inquebrantable modelo, buscando progresar desde atrás, y protagonizó alguna que otra salida interesante. El combinado dirigido por Dick Schreuder, extécnico del Castellón, se fue sintiendo cada vez más cómodo con el paso de los minutos. Ouaissa, incluso, llegó a toparse con la madera... aunque Sánchez Martínez invalidó la acción por fuera de juego. Fue, eso sí, un toque de atención bastante serio para un Olympiacos que buscó responder con varios disparos lejanos que permitieron lucirse a Crettaz. Mendilibar sentía la necesidad de introducir alguna modificación para afrontar la segunda parte: Joel Roca se quedó en el vestuario y Gelson Martins ocupó su lugar. No tardó el ex del Atlético en realizar su primera incursión a línea de fondo y, acto seguido, tuvo un mano a mano... en posición adelantada. Jamiro Monteiro, presente en el Mundial con Cabo Verde, también tanteó a Popovic. Quedó claro durante el desarrollo de la segunda parte que ambos equipos todavía se están 'desengrasando'. Cada vez había más espacios entre líneas... pero ninguno terminó de estar del todo fino para intentar desnivelar una eliminatoria que se resolverá la próxima semana en Países Bajos. Mucho más animado, sin duda, estuvo el encuentro de ida entre Union SG y Bodo/Glimt (3-3), dos equipos que ya disputaron la pasada Champions y de donde saldrá el rival de Olympiacos o NEC Nimega. El capitán Patrick Berg abrió el marcador en el 25', Florucz igualó poco después, Blomberg no desaprovechó un penalti para volver a adelantar a los de Knutsen... y Florucz volvió a aparecer para firmar el 2-2 en el descuento de la primera parte. Promise David, en el 88', hizo saltar todo por los aires. Pero Bjortuft acabó rescatando un empate para el Bodo en el 91'. El gran 'traspiés' de la noche, seguramente, lo protagonizó un Olympique de Lyon que se hundió en República Checa contra el Sparta Praga (2-1). Se las prometían muy felices los de Paulo Fonseca con el gol anulado a Brunnes y el anotado en propia por Suchomel al filo del descanso. Pero, superada la hora de encuentro, los goles en Rynes (63') y Mercado (69') les hicieron colapsar. Tolisso, entre medias, desperdició un penaltis Partidos de la tercera ronda previa de la Champions 26-27: No fue la noche de Mendilibar... pero sí la de Julio Velázquez. Tras superar a Borac y Universitatea Craiova en las dos primeras rondas previas de la Champions, un solitario tanto a cargo de Serginho en el tiempo de descuento inclinó la balanza en favor de su Levski Sofía frente al Kairat (1-0), donde Marc Gual volvió a ser de la partida. Kazajistán decidirá si llegan a la última fase previa al sorteo, donde ya espera el AEK Atenas. También le fue bien la jornada a Sergi Domínguez, titular en el eje de la zaga de un Dinamo Zagreb que no dio opción alguna al Kauno Zalgiris (5-0) y dejó la eliminatoria prácticamente resuelta. Todo lo contrario al Estrella Roja, que no encontró la manera de remontar a un Happoel Be'er Sheva (1-0) que disputó la última media hora con un futbolista menos. La caldera del Rajko Mitic deberá prenderse la próxima semana en busca de darle la vuelta al cruce. Un escenario que también aplica para el Celje, que cayó ante el Ararat (2-1). Lleno hasta la bandera, prácticamente multiplicando por 10 a la población censada en Hällevik, estaba el estadio del humilde Mjällby sueco para recibir la visita del Slovan Bratislava de Yayá Touré, que tuvo que esperar al descuento para remontar el choque (1-2) y tomar ventaja en la eliminatoria de cara a la vuelta en Eslovaquia. Mientras haya vida, seguirán teniendo esperanza.

articles.title: Asensio quiere Champions
articles.standfirst: El '10' de Fenerbahçe sirvió una asistencia en favor de Greenwood que amarró la victoria contra el Sturm Graz (2-0) en la ida de la tercera ronda previa de la Champions
articles.summary: El '10' de Fenerbahçe sirvió una asistencia en favor de Greenwood que amarró la victoria contra el Sturm Graz (2-0) en la ida de la tercera ronda previa de la Champions
articles.body: Seguro que Asensio y todo Fenerbahçe celebraron la derrota contra el Sparta Praga por parte de un Olympique de Lyon al que querían esquivar a toda costa en la última fase previa de la Champions. Sin embargo, hoy les tocaba responder a ellos... y tomaron ventaja en la eliminatoria contra el Sturm Graz (2-0). Asensio, junto a Kanté y Guendouzi, fue titular en la sala de máquinas y gozó de plena libertad para asociarse con Mason Greenwood, Aktürkoglü y un Anderson Talisca que, con Muriqi en el banquillo, ejerció como '9'. Al brasileño le llevó menos de 10' estrenar el marcador tras conectar un potente remate cruzado desde la frontal. Justo al llegar a la primera media hora de encuentro, el Fenerbahçe se llevó dos buenos sustos. El primero, en forma de lesión de Oosterwolde; y el segundo a razón de un pisotón de Skriniar sobre Jatta en el interior del área. Chris Kavanagh, sin embargo, no consideró que fuese suficiente para pitar penalti. Partidos de la tercera ronda previa de la Champions 26-27: Había bajado el ritmo Fenerbahçe. Pero, antes de emprender el camino al túnel de vestuarios, Greenwood sacó a lucir el cañón que con el que cuenta en su pierna izquierda. Recibió en el 'piquito' del área un saque de esquina 'botado' por un Marco Asensio que viene de repartir 13 asistencias el curso pasado, se percató que nadie le 'flotaba' y 'fusiló' por el palo corto. No se conformaba Fenerbahçe... ni tampoco Asensio, que dejó mano a mano a Talisca antes de abandonar el terreno de juego a falta de poco más de 20'. Ismail Kartal también retiró a Greenwood y aprovechó para equilibrar el equipo con la entrada de Fred en la sala de máquinas. La renta era valiosa y quería conservarla de cara a la vuelta en Austria. La Champions está un pasito más cerca.

articles.title: La UEFA cambia el ciclo de amarillas en las competiciones europeas
articles.standfirst: La organización efectuará cambios en la normativa sobre las amonestaciones en los tres torneos
articles.summary: La organización efectuará cambios en la normativa sobre las amonestaciones en los tres torneos
articles.body: La UEFA ha tomado una decisión que cambiará el devenir de las tres competiciones europeas internacionales. La organización ha decidido tomar una decisión que afectará directamente al sistema de acumulación de tarjetas amarillas durante la fase de clasificación de la Champions, Europa League y Conference.  En el 'nuevo' formato que se implantó hace ya dos temporadas se juegan ocho encuentros en la fase de clasificación, por lo que la UEFA ha decidido implementar una nueva norma en la que los jugadores tendrán que ver una cartulina amarilla más para perderse el siguiente encuentro. La organización ha decidido que los futbolistas no cumplan sanción hasta acumular cuatro tarjetas amarillas, en vez de tres como estaba estipulado en la normativa anterior. En la próxima edición cuando un futbolista sea amonestado en cuatro partidos de la fase de clasificación cumplirá un encuentro de sanción.  De esta forma tanto los equipos como jugadores tendrán más flexibilidad a la hora de plantearse los encuentros.

articles.title: Leicester City: Premier League title moments - a decade on
articles.summary: Leicester are gearing up for League One but 10 years ago they were defending Premier League champions. The dream moments haven't been forgotten.
articles.body:
It was a dream then, it is a dream now - especially as Leicester prepare for League One.

Ten years ago the Foxes were preparing to defend their Premier League title and looking forward to Champions League football.

At 5,000-1, they had pulled off the most improbable, the most stunning, the most incredible feat to shock the world.

But now, after back-to-back relegations, those days seem almost as surreal as when they actually happened.

New manager Russell Martin will be expected to take the club back to the Championship at the first attempt, something that sounds nowhere near as impossible as what the Foxes previously managed.

A decade on, the 'pinch-me' moments live on for those who were there, and some have shared them with BBC Sport.

Spoiler: they might not be the ones you knew about.

Leicester had won the title without kicking a ball on 2 May 2016 when nearest challengers Tottenham Hotspur could only manage a 2-2 draw with Chelsea .

The next day, there was only one group of men the media wanted to speak to.

Crowds gathered at the club's former training ground at Belvoir Drive, a few miles outside the centre of Leicester.

Journalists and fans waited - one cameraman persuaded a neighbour to allow him in to film from their bathroom window as he aimed to get footage of the celebrating Foxes.

The media were finally instructed to head to King Power Stadium where the press room would be opened.

A five-minute drive took 30 minutes through revelling fans and it was a battle to get to there but, inside, the world's media edged in, hoping to hear from those who made this miracle possible.

But only eight reporters would receive a secret invitation to head back to Belvoir Drive.

Quietly, one-by-one, the handpicked members of the British press who regularly covered the club, slipped out of the packed room and made their way back.

This time, they were let in and ushered into the family room, just to the right of reception.

When manager Claudio Ranieri walked in, he received an immediate, impromptu, standing ovation and shook hands with those who had watched the astounding season unfold.

The man the world wanted to speak to gave an engaging audience to a few writers for 45 minutes.

Ranieri had been a left-field appointment at the start of that season, having not managed in England for 12 years since leaving Chelsea in 2004.

And he had considered bringing in some unconventional methods, such as double training sessions, which were nipped in the bud with the help of Craig Shakespeare, who had stayed on as assistant after the sacking of Ranieri's predecessor Nigel Pearson.

There were off-field changes he would bring in, though, including taking the squad out to make their own pizza after the first clean sheet of the season against Crystal Palace in October 2015.

"It sounds funny - we're keeping a clean sheet and gone for pizza but you then end up speaking to someone in the squad you probably wouldn't have spoken to at training because there's 25 of you," says former centre-back Robert Huth.

"You train, but you don't really know the guy. How's he functioning? Does he like me to shout at him? Does he want me to just be quiet?

"You talk and go through the game where maybe you wouldn't mention things, like a problem that you see on a pitch, if it's like, a stiff environment.

"If you're out and about, and you go: 'When the ball's here, I prefer if you do this' - just like tiny little things and you take criticism on differently when you talk in a social environment. You don't want to sit in a meeting room being told what to do."

It allowed winger Riyad Mahrez to flourish and Jamie Vardy to plunder 24 league goals, with Ranieri comparing his counter-attacking forwards to the RAF.

It is well documented that Vardy had invited the squad to his house to watch what would end up being the title-winning match as Spurs blew a 2-0 lead to draw with Chelsea - and that some players needed to wait at the local police station before arriving because of the crowds of fans who had gathered outside.

While everyone else partied, winger Nathan Dyer had a different night, in hospital with wife Laura after the birth of their second child, Shea, two days earlier.

"I had the laptop out watching the game in hospital, the boys were at the party. I wasn't able to make it but I'd never miss the birth of my child," he says.

"It was a strange feeling. It was surreal, like it wasn't real at the time but it was.

"We had to be put in a room as people were putting their heads round and even then you could see the eyes at the door. People were congratulating me and were really proud.

"It was the whole city, even people who were not fans were so happy Leicester had achieved this."

He'd had a dramatic arrival at the club in the first place that season, joining on loan from Swansea on transfer deadline day and being flown to Leicester in the late former owner Khun Vichai's helicopter to beat the deadline.

"My wife was pregnant, we'd just moved into a new house, so everything was in boxes, it was a wild day," he says.

"It was exciting for me but also nerve-wracking because it was so intense, to send the helicopter to get me to get it over the line. It was a proud moment for me - I'd always wanted to be involved in a moment like that, watching on the TV - breaking news!"

Leicester were two points behind Arsenal at the turn of the year but one defeat in the final 16 games - a dramatic late loss at Arsenal in February - had put them on course for the title.

The closer they edged to the impossible, the more the interest in the Foxes exploded.

Vardy had a lookalike - postman Lee Chapman - and Ranieri had a sausage named after him.

Local butchers W Archer & Son created the Ranieri from Packington free-range pork, fennel, garlic and chilli.

It won a star at the Great Taste awards and at one stage the shop was shifting 12kg (26.5lb) a day.

Owner Sean Jeynes even brought a plate of sausages to the stadium before a news conference, which led Ranieri to declare himself 'the sausageman'.

"It was surreal that day. How did that ever happen?" says Jeynes.

"We were making sausages two or three times a day, smelling of garlic, smelling of fennel, but it was just a crazy time. It really was a crazy time - you can't quite comprehend what it was like.

"It had a massive effect on the city, it had a great effect on everybody. Everyone was much happier.

"Nothing can replace the Italian sausage, the recipe, and the pork, fennel, garlic chili and a hint of Champions League.

"People would say, why don't you do a [Brendan] Rodgers sausage [after winning the FA Cup in 2021], but it's just not the same."

The sausage is still occasionally back on their counters, a lasting reminder of a unique time.

That is not the only taste of success that is still being enjoyed today.

"Thanks to Leicester City it meant I could retire at 55 instead of 67," says Foxes Trust co-chair Lynn Wyeth, who stuck Â£2 on the club at odds of 5,000-1 at the start of the season.

"It was actually really stressful. A first world problem, isn't it? It was stressful enough, watching them get closer and closer thinking, oh my god, can we do it? But knowing that there was Â£10,000 riding on it as well, was like, 'oh, no, I almost wish I'd cashed out earlier'.

"When I won, I had my account shut for money laundering, I had to prove it was me and that I'd won it.

"We managed to clear it up quite quickly, I think it's just an automatic thing.

articles.title: Carabao Cup 2026-27: When is the third-round draw and which teams are in it?
articles.summary: The third-round draw of the EFL Cup takes place on Wednesday, with nine Premier League teams entering the competition at this stage.
articles.body:
The third-round draw for the 2026-27 Carabao Cup will take place on Wednesday, 26 August following the conclusion of Preston North End vs Everton.

Nine Premier League clubs taking part in European football join the 23 first-round winners from across the English Football League.

Arsenal, Manchester City, Manchester United, Aston Villa, Liverpool, Bournemouth, Sunderland, Brighton and Crystal Palace will enter the competition at this stage, as the top eight Premier League clubs from the 2025-26 season plus Crystal Palace as Conference League winners.

It will be broadcast live on Sky Sports following the conclusion of the third round tie between Preston North End and Everton, kicking off at 20:00 BST that evening.

Unlike the opening two rounds of the competition, the third round draw is not regionalised.

However, before the match at Deepdale there will be a pre-draw determining which of the Champions League and Europa League clubs will play at home or away in round three.

In order to avoid potential scheduling issues, the eight Champions League and Europa League clubs cannot be drawn against each other in round three.

When the draw takes place, the first eight fixtures decided are the ones involving clubs in the Champions League and Europa League. The remainder of the draw will be an open draw as usual.

Due to clashes with opening weeks of the Champions League and Europa League seasons, the third round will be played across two different weeks. They are the weeks commencing Monday, 7 and Monday, 14 September, 2026.

articles.title: Transfer window: What's it like being a partner of a footballer on deadline day?
articles.summary: What is life like for footballers' families during the transfer window where a last-minute deal means you need to uproot your life and move hundreds of miles?
articles.body:
"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

articles.title: Luis Enrique, ante un 'récord único': "Podemos igualar al Real Madrid"
articles.standfirst: El técnico español prepara el nuevo curso con la ambición de igualar a los blancos, el único club capaz de conquistar tres Champions consecutivas
articles.summary: El técnico español prepara el nuevo curso con la ambición de igualar a los blancos, el único club capaz de conquistar tres Champions consecutivas
articles.body: Después de un largo parón y un descanso revitalizador para jugadores y cuerpo técnico, la temporada ya se presenta a la vuelta de la esquina. Los clubes afrontan sus últimos test de la pretemporada, una oportunidad ideal para pulir detalles y llegar en el mejor estado de forma posible al inicio de la competición. Luis Enrique habló sobre este "descanso". A pesar de haber pasado unas semanas fuera de París con su familia, el técnico afirma que desconectar al 100 % es imposible. “Siempre estás conectado porque todo el mundo te habla de la temporada y te felicita por lo que has ganado”. Aunque pueda resulta agradable ver a la gente satisfecha con los éxitos, la realidad de la profesión es distinta. “Demuestra que un entrenador nunca desconecta del todo. Hay que tomar muchas decisiones en verano, no vas a tu lugar de trabajo, pero sigues conectado con el club”, afirmó el exjugador de Barça y Madrid a la UEFA . Quizá sea esa constancia y persistencia lo que ha llevado a Luis Enrique a conquistar dos Champions consecutivas y a colocar al PSG en el centro de la escena internacional como gran favorito. “No soy un genio y no quiero serlo”, desveló el entrenador. “Tengo una obsesión constante por intentar mejorar el rendimiento, mi conexión con los jugadores y con el equipo, además de afrontar las exigencias que se me plantean”. Por ello, antes de pensar en el futuro, deberá preparar su primera gran prueba del curso. Este miércoles se enfrentará al Aston Villa en la Supercopa de la UEFA, un título al que el técnico otorga la máxima importancia con el objetivo de revalidarlo, tal como hizo el año pasado frente al Tottenham. "No me cabe ninguna duda de que la Supercopa es un trofeo realmente importante y que el Villa será muy competitivo", reconoció. Sin embargo, su ambición va mucho más allá. Y es que el asturiano está ante la oportunidad de igualar un récord histórico que solo ostenta el Real Madrid: conquistar tres Champions League consecutivas. El propio Luis Enrique se mostró entusiasmado ante tal posibilidad. “Ahora mismo tenemos un reto único, algo prácticamente sin precedentes en la historia del fútbol europeo: igualar al Real Madrid si conseguimos ganar una tercera Liga de Campeones consecutiva. ¡Vaya! Es otro nivel. Nadie en la historia ha ganado tres seguidas, excepto el Real Madrid”. Aunque es consciente de la dificultad de la gesta. “Nadie en la historia ha ganado tres seguidas, excepto el Real Madrid”, asegura que la ambición del grupo es máxima. “No creo que haya un solo equipo en Europa más motivado que nosotros”. El técnico confía ciegamente en las posibilidades de su plantilla. “Es el proyecto en el que más he invertido”, señaló, aunque siempre manteniendo los pies en el suelo. “Hoy, cuando me dicen: ‘Has ganado muchos títulos’, respondo que no importa; es el pasado, es historia antigua”, concluyó.
